studies.title: Hearts Turned To Play
studies.meaning: The surah opens on a mismatch. Something is described as having drawn near, and the people it concerns are facing the other way. Then the diagnosis narrows twice: they hear the reminder, but they hear it as entertainment, and their hearts are elsewhere while they listen. Only after that does the passage report what they actually say, and it turns out to be a private conversation about whether a man like themselves could be anything at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah belongs to a period when the message had been public long enough to be familiar, and the opposition had settled into dismissal rather than alarm. The picture of men conferring quietly and then putting a rhetorical question to a crowd matches what other passages report of Meccan leaders coordinating their response. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A verb of approach placed first in the sentence for emphasis. It occurs twice in this surah, here of the reckoning and near the end of the true promise, framing everything between them.
This word occurs only here. It describes a heart absorbed in something else rather than one refusing, so the fault named is attention drifting rather than a decision being made.
Said of the reminder as it comes. Revelation is described as arriving in instalments, each one new when it lands, which is what makes the repeated failure to attend so pointed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's evenings ran on talk. Men gathered in the courtyards around the sanctuary, poetry was recited and judged, news from the caravans was traded, and a new voice was an event to be sampled. Recitation was one entertainment among several. The complaint here is not that they refused to listen but that they listened in exactly the way they listened to everything else.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that opens this surah, saying that something has drawn near, returns near its close, where the true promise is described in the same word. The surah is bracketed by it. Everything between those two points, including the long gallery of prophets the surah is named for, sits inside a single announcement that time is shorter than the audience assumes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a failure that is not disbelief. These people listen, and what disqualifies them is the manner of the listening: playfully, with the heart occupied elsewhere. That makes attention itself a moral category rather than a preliminary to one. It also implies that the ordinary danger for anyone who has heard the message often is not rejecting it but becoming an audience for it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same opening verb near the end of this surah, of the true promise drawing near.
Uses the same phrase for a freshly arrived reminder and reports the same turning away from it.
Opens another surah with the same verb of approach, there of the hour itself.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you listen to something familiar today, a recitation, a talk, a passage you know. Catch the moment your attention slides while your ears stay open. Do not scold yourself for it. Just mark it, because this ayah says the drifting, not the disagreeing, is what it is describing.

studies.title: A Jumble Of Dreams
studies.meaning: The reply to a private conversation is that nothing said anywhere is private, and it ends on two names about hearing and knowing. Then the objections come in a rush, each introduced by a particle that abandons the last one. It is confused dreaming, no, he invented it, no, he is a poet, and then a demand for the kind of sign earlier peoples received. Commentators note that the three charges contradict each other, which is itself the point of listing them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Reports of this period describe Meccan leaders trying out different explanations for the recitation and settling on none, since a man who was dreaming could not also be a deliberate forger. Poetry was the recognised category for powerful speech, so calling him a poet was an attempt to file the Quran somewhere familiar. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these two ayat.

keyTerms.note: A word for a mixed handful of stalks or grass tied together. Applied to dreams it means images with no coherent thread, and the phrase occurs only twice in the Quran.
A verb for cutting and stitching something together, used of invented speech. It accuses him of deliberate work, which is the opposite of the charge in the phrase just before it.
In seventh-century Arabia a poet was a public figure with a recognised gift, sometimes credited with contact with unseen forces. The label was not an insult but an attempt at classification.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was the closest thing Arabia had to institutional authority in language. Tribes kept poets the way later states kept lawyers, and a good verse could make a reputation or ruin one at the seasonal fairs. Meccans knew the metres by ear from childhood. That is why the charge could be made and also why it failed: the audience could hear that the recitation did not scan like poetry.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here to dismiss the revelation as confused dreams occurs in only one other place in the Quran, where Egyptian courtiers use it to dismiss a king's dream that turns out to be a true warning of famine. In both places the words are spoken confidently by people who are about to be shown to have missed something.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply given first is about knowledge, not about evidence. Their private conferring is answered by saying that speech anywhere is heard, which relocates the argument from public debate to what people say when they think no one is listening. The three accusations that follow are left uncorrected, and their incompatibility is allowed to stand as the answer. Rejection here is shown to be a conclusion looking for a reason.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for confused dreams, of a warning the courtiers could not read.
Answers the same two charges directly, that it is not the speech of a poet nor of a soothsayer.
Reports the same labels being applied and the same waiting for something to befall him.

studies.applyIt: Listen for incompatible reasons the next time you hear something dismissed, in a meeting, a family argument, or your own head. When the objections do not fit together, the conclusion usually came first. Try noticing it once in your own case today, on something small you have already decided you do not want to do.

studies.title: Men Who Ate Food
studies.meaning: Three answers are given to the demand for a sign. First, earlier towns that received signs did not believe, so the request would not do what it claims. Second, every messenger before was a man, and the audience is told to ask those who keep the earlier records if they doubt it. Third, none of them was a body that did not eat, and none of them lived forever. The objection assumed prophecy meant something other than a human life.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The complaint that a messenger should not be an ordinary man who walks in markets is reported repeatedly from this period. Jewish and Christian communities on the trade routes north held written records of earlier prophets, and the instruction to ask those who possess the reminder appeals to that knowledge. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: The plain word for men, chosen against every alternative the language offered. Prophecy is defined here by what the messengers were not: not angels, not immortals, not bodies exempt from eating.
Those who hold the earlier record. The phrase occurs twice in the Quran and in both places it sends questioners to a body of knowledge outside the immediate dispute.
The Quran uses this word for a form that does not live as a person does. Denying that prophets were such bodies insists that they hungered, aged and died like everyone listening.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Eating was public in Arabia and it placed you. Who slaughtered for whom, who ate at whose fire, who could afford meat and who lived on dates and barley was known to everyone in a small town. A man who did not eat would have stood outside the whole social order. Insisting that the messengers ate meant insisting they were inside it, with obligations to hosts and neighbours.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to ask the people of the reminder occurs twice in the Quran, and both times it follows the identical statement that God sent only men before, inspired by Him. The two passages are almost word for word, in two different surahs of the same period, which is unusual even among the Quran's many parallel formulations.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is defined downward here, by subtraction. The messenger is not exempt from hunger, not exempt from death, and not exempt from being an ordinary member of a community. That protects two things at once. It keeps the message from depending on a spectacle, and it makes the messenger's life imitable, since nothing he did was done with a body unlike the reader's own.

crossReferences.why: Gives almost the identical statement and the same instruction to ask those who hold the reminder.
Reports the objection this answers, that the messenger eats food and walks in the markets.
States a few ayat later that no human before him was granted permanence, the same denial applied directly.

studies.applyIt: Take one person whose example you find impossible and check what you have quietly assumed about them: that they had more time, better health, an easier temperament. Then look for the evidence. This passage insists that the people worth following were hungry, tired and mortal, which is the only reason following them is possible.

studies.title: And We Raised Another People
studies.meaning: A promise is described as having been made good, and the rescue that follows has a wider reach than expected: the messengers, and whoever God willed besides them. Those destroyed are named by a single fault, going past all measure. Then a book is mentioned that contains the audience's own reminder, and the passage returns to history with a verb of breaking. Towns were shattered and other peoples raised in their place, which makes replacement, not merely ruin, the point.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is answering a demand for a sign by pointing at what happened to earlier peoples who received one. Mecca's own prosperity rested on a position its inhabitants had inherited rather than won, and other tribes had held the sanctuary before them. The claim that populations are replaced was not theoretical to that audience. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.gloss: those who go past all measure
keyTerms.note: From a verb for exceeding the proper limit, in spending or in anything else. It names the destroyed not by their beliefs but by a manner of living, which is a broader charge than disbelief.
The word carries both a reminder and a mention that raises someone's standing. Commentators note both readings, so the book is at once what recalls them and what their reputation rests on.
A verb for snapping something hard, like a bone or a staff. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it describes destruction as a fracture rather than as a burning or a drowning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca knew that custodianship changed hands. The tribes that had held the sanctuary and its water before Quraysh were remembered by name, and the arrangement that gave the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) his own clan its standing was a few generations old at most. Every family could recite a genealogy that included someone else's decline. Being told that peoples are replaced described a process they could trace.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for shattering a town occurs only once in the whole Quran. It comes from the physical vocabulary of breaking something rigid, a staff or a bone, and Arabic uses it for a fracture that cannot be set. The surah applies it to a settlement, and then in the same breath describes another people being brought into being in its place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes continuity, not only judgement, the subject. What follows destruction is not emptiness but another community with the same opportunity, which frames history as a sequence of chances rather than a record of verdicts. The mention of the book in the middle of that sequence is deliberate: the reader is being shown where in the pattern they currently stand, with the reminder already in hand.

crossReferences.why: Describes generations established and then destroyed, with another generation raised after them.
States the same rule about deliverance, that saving the messengers and the believers is binding upon Us.
Uses the same word for a reminder that is also an honour, and says you will be questioned about it.

studies.applyIt: Read the middle ayah as addressed to you: the book contains your reminder. Open it once today at a place you did not choose in advance, and read a few lines as though they were meant for the position you are actually in. The passage is not describing a general truth about scripture. It is locating you inside a sequence.

studies.title: Go Back To Your Comforts
studies.meaning: The scene is set at the moment of realisation. They feel the force coming and they run, and the sentence that answers them is heavy with irony: do not run, go back to your comforts and your houses, so that you may be questioned. Commentators read the summons as mocking the assumption that a life of ease entitles a person to be consulted. Their answer is a single cry admitting they were the wrongdoers, and it continues until nothing is left.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage generalises what happened to earlier towns rather than naming one, which is the surah's method throughout this section. Its listeners were the leading families of a trading city whose houses and imported goods marked them out. The picture of prosperous men running from their own streets was aimed at a specific audience without accusing anyone by name. No occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for the swift striking of legs, used of a horse at speed. Its root occurs three times in the Quran, twice in these two lines and once when Job is told to strike the ground with his foot.
A passive form: the comfort was conferred on them, not built by them. The root describes a softness produced by abundance, the condition of people whose wealth has removed all friction from life.
The word for a fire that has gone out, leaving no flame and no sound. It occurs only here, and it ends the scene with an image of silence rather than of destruction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A prosperous Meccan house announced itself. Imported cloth from Yemen, vessels from Syria, a courtyard with room for guests, and slaves to fetch water from wells other families queued at. These were the visible returns on the caravan trade. Being told to run back to those rooms, because there were questions to answer there, turned the whole display into a summons rather than an achievement.
studies.didYouKnow: The cry these people make, admitting they were wrongdoers, returns almost word for word near the end of this surah, where those who disbelieved say it on the day their eyes fix in horror. The surah puts the same sentence in the mouths of a doomed town and of everyone at the resurrection, so history and the last day produce identical speech.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The summons back to the houses is the passage's sharpest move. It does not deny that they were comfortable; it treats the comfort as a position that carries an account. That is a different claim from saying wealth is wrong. It also shows recognition arriving intact and too late: they name their fault accurately, in the correct words, at the one moment when naming it changes nothing.

crossReferences.why: Puts nearly the same admission in the mouths of those facing the true promise at the end of this surah.
Describes those given ease in a town being the first to act corruptly when a warning arrives.
Reports that the ones given ease in every warned town were the ones who rejected the message.

studies.applyIt: Pick one comfort you have stopped noticing: hot water, a car that starts, a fridge with food in it. Say once today, plainly, that it was given rather than earned. Not to feel guilty about it. The ayah's point is that ease comes with a conversation attached, and the conversation is easier to have early.

studies.title: Not Created In Play
studies.meaning: A denial about the universe is followed by a strange concession. Creation was not made as entertainment, and if amusement had been wanted, it could have been found without making anything. The point is that the world is not a diversion for its maker. Then the tone changes to violence: truth is hurled at falsehood and knocks it out, and falsehood simply goes. Commentators note the verb is one of physical impact, not of argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just described a town realising too late that its comforts were a question rather than an answer, and the objection this passage meets is the assumption that nothing is at stake. That assumption underwrote the mood of the surah's opening, where the reminder was heard playfully. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these three ayat.

keyTerms.note: The word occurs twice in this surah. Here creation is denied as play, and later Abraham's people ask whether he is only playing with them, so the same idea is tested from both ends.
This verb occurs only here. It means to strike the skull hard enough to reach the brain, so the image is a killing blow rather than a refutation or an exposure.
Used of something departing or perishing, including of a life leaving a body. Falsehood is not corrected in this picture; it simply stops being there.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Amusement in Arabia was the privilege of the settled and the rich. Poetry contests, gambling with arrows for portions of a slaughtered camel, wine and singing girls belonged to men with leisure and surplus. The word used here for the diversion God does not need was the word for exactly that world. Saying creation is not that kind of thing addressed people who organised their evenings around it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word denying that creation is play appears twice in this surah. It is used here of God, and later of Abraham, when his people ask whether he is telling the truth or only playing with them. It occurs once more in the Quran, in another surah, making the identical statement about the heavens and the earth.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage rules out two ideas at once: that the world is a toy, and that its maker needed anything from making it. What replaces play is not sternness but seriousness, which is a different quality. The image that follows says something about how falsehood ends. It is not refuted into agreement or slowly persuaded away. It is struck, and what struck it was the truth arriving, not an argument winning.

crossReferences.why: States the identical denial about the heavens and the earth, adding that they were created with truth.
Uses the same word later in this surah, when Abraham's people ask whether he is merely playing.
Gives the same picture of truth arriving and falsehood departing, since falsehood is bound to vanish.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you are treating as low-stakes because nobody is checking: a habit, a promise, an hour. Ask what it would look like to hold it as though it counted. Not more anxiously, only more seriously. The passage does not say the world is grim. It says it is not a diversion, which is a different thing entirely.

studies.title: They Do Not Grow Weary
studies.meaning: Ownership is stated first, then the behaviour of those nearest is described by three denials. They are not too proud to serve, they do not become exhausted, and they do not slacken. The passage does not say they love it or find it easy; it says fatigue does not enter. That description is then turned into a question. If those closest to God serve without wearying, what exactly are gods taken from the earth supposed to be able to do.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Some in Mecca held that the angels were daughters of God or intermediaries who could be petitioned, and several surahs of this period address that belief without polemic against any group. The question that closes this passage tests the claim on its own terms rather than dismissing it. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: This verb occurs only here. Its root is used of a camel driven until it collapses and cannot rise, so what is denied is not boredom but the total giving out of strength.
From a root for swimming or moving freely through something. Glorification is pictured as continuous motion rather than as repeated acts, which fits the denial of tiring that follows.
A verb for spreading out and reviving, used of the earth after rain and of bodies being brought back. The question asks whether any earthly god has ever done the one thing that matters.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Exhaustion was the limit of every Arabian enterprise. A camel could be pushed only so far before it foundered, a well yielded only so much before it needed a night to refill, and a man on watch could hold out until dawn and no longer. Everything the audience relied on had a point at which it gave out. Service that never reached that point was the genuinely strange claim in this passage.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb denying that those near God become exhausted occurs only once in the Quran, here. It is built on a root that Arabic uses for a beast driven past its endurance until it drops, and the same root supplies a word for the eye straining and returning defeated, which appears in a surah about looking at the sky for a flaw.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Worship is described here without any reference to reward or feeling, and defined instead by the absence of two failures: pride and fatigue. That makes constancy, rather than intensity, the mark of nearness. The turn at the end also does real work. It moves from a description of what the nearest creatures do to a question about what the alleged rivals have ever done, and answers it by silence.

crossReferences.why: Says those with your Lord glorify Him night and day and do not grow weary of it.
Uses the same root for a gaze that returns exhausted after searching the sky for any flaw.
Continues this description a few ayat later, calling them honoured servants who do not speak before He does.

studies.applyIt: Pick the smallest possible act of remembrance, a single phrase, and attach it to something you already do many times a day: unlocking your phone, filling a glass. The passage measures nearness by not stopping rather than by effort. Choose something so light that tiring is not a factor, and let the repetition be the whole of it.

studies.title: They Would Both Have Gone To Ruin
studies.meaning: An argument is compressed into a single conditional. Had there been other gods in the heavens and the earth, both would have fallen into disorder. Commentators explain the reasoning as a matter of competing wills: two authorities with real power cannot both have the last word, and a universe that holds together is evidence that one does. The next line then removes the last handle anyone might reach for. He is not questioned about what He does, and everyone else is.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is in the middle of a sustained argument against gods taken alongside God, addressed to an audience whose sanctuary held many objects of devotion and who did not deny God's existence at all. The argument therefore targets partnership rather than atheism. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these two ayat.

keyTerms.gloss: both would have gone to ruin
keyTerms.note: A dual verb from a root for something spoiling or breaking down, used of food going bad and of order collapsing. The dual keeps heaven and earth together, so the ruin covers the whole arrangement.
The Quran's image for the seat of sovereignty. Naming God Lord of the Throne in this sentence answers the question of authority directly, since a throne admits one occupant.

A verb for giving an account of something, as a merchant describes goods he is selling. It treats the claims about God as descriptions offered rather than as beliefs held, which is a cooler way of putting it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Divided authority was Arabia's chronic problem. Mecca had no king and no court; it was run by an assembly of clan leaders whose agreements held only while interests aligned, and feuds ran for decades because no one could impose a settlement. The audience did not need the argument explained. They had watched what happens to a valley with several men who each believe they decide.
studies.didYouKnow: The argument in this ayah is made in a clause of seven Arabic words, and the Quran gives a longer version of it in another surah, where each god would have taken away what it created and some would have overcome others. Here the reasoning is left entirely implicit, and the classical commentaries reconstruct it from that single conditional.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Oneness is argued from the world rather than asserted from revelation, which makes the claim testable in principle. The second ayah then draws the consequence most people would rather avoid: being beyond question is part of what it means to be God. That is stated without softening, and the sentence balances it immediately by saying that everyone else will be questioned, so nobody is exempt from the accounting except the one who runs it.

crossReferences.why: Spells out the same argument at length, with each god carrying off what it made and overcoming the rest.
Puts the case differently, that other gods would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.
Establishes a few lines earlier that everyone in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you are running two authorities at once: what you say you value and what actually decides your week. You do not need to resolve it today. Just write both down on the same page and look at them, because the ayah's claim is that competing authorities do not coexist quietly for long.

studies.title: Bring Your Proof
studies.meaning: The demand is turned around. Instead of defending its own claim, the passage asks the other side for evidence, using a word from the vocabulary of legal proof. Then it points at two things at once: this message, and the message of those who came before, treating both as a record available for inspection. The ayah closes with a diagnosis rather than a verdict. Most of them do not know the truth, and what follows from that is turning away.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been arguing against gods taken alongside God for several ayat, and here it shifts the burden. Mecca's religion rested on inherited practice rather than on argument, and demanding proof was an unfamiliar move in a society where the strongest reason for anything was that the fathers had done it. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: A word for decisive proof, the kind that settles a case rather than supports a view. The Quran uses the same demand four times, always addressed to a claim that rests on custom rather than reason.
The same word the surah has already used for the revelation and for the honour it confers. Here it names two bodies of testimony, the present one and the earlier one, as a single line of evidence.
The word that closed the surah's opening ayah, returning here. Not knowing and turning away are joined by the sentence, so the aversion is presented as the consequence of the ignorance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan disputes were settled by evidence in exactly this sense. A man claiming a debt or a share in a caravan brought witnesses, and a claim without them failed no matter how loudly it was pressed. The vocabulary of proof belonged to the market and the assembly. Asking for it about the gods in the sanctuary applied an everyday standard to the one area where nobody had ever applied it.
studies.didYouKnow: The demand to produce your proof occurs four times in the Quran, and in each of those places it answers a claim about partners beside God or about the hereafter. Three of the four appear in surahs of this same Meccan period. The Quran uses the word for a decisive legal proof, not the ordinary word for an argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats belief as something that can be asked to account for itself, and it applies that standard to the opposing side rather than exempting its own. Pointing at the earlier record alongside the present one also makes a claim about continuity: what is being offered is not a novelty but the latest entry in a series. The final clause is generous in a hard way, naming ignorance rather than malice as the problem.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical demand against a claim about who enters the garden, asking for proof if they are truthful.
Makes the same demand at the end of a list of things only God does, asking for proof of any partner.
Opens this surah with the same word for turning away that closes this ayah.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you believe because you have always believed it, not a matter of faith necessarily, anything: about your abilities, about a relative, about how a situation must go. Ask what your proof is. If there is a good one, you will find it. If there is not, you have learned something the ayah is inviting you to learn.

studies.title: Honoured Servants
studies.meaning: One sentence is said to have been given to every messenger without exception, and it is put in the first person, so the reader hears it as God speaking rather than as a doctrine reported. Then a specific claim is answered. Some had said the Merciful has taken a child, and the reply corrects the category rather than the detail: they are honoured servants. Two behaviours follow, and both are about precedence. They do not speak ahead of Him, and they act on His command.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Beliefs about the angels as daughters of God circulated in Mecca and are addressed in several surahs of this period. The reply here is unusually gentle in its wording, correcting the relation while calling them honoured, and it avoids naming any group. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat, which continue the argument begun with the demand for proof.

keyTerms.note: A command in the first person, the same words that end the message given to every messenger. It appears again later in this surah, closing the account of the prophets with the same instruction.
A passive participle: honour conferred on them rather than possessed by them. The word grants everything the mistaken claim wanted, dignity and nearness, while removing the relationship it assumed.

A verb from racing, of one runner getting ahead of another. Applied to speech, it describes not saying anything before the one who decides has spoken, which is a picture of restraint rather than obedience.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Precedence governed every Arabian gathering. Who spoke first in an assembly, who was greeted first, who entered a tent ahead of whom, all of it followed a known order, and a man who spoke before his senior committed a real offence. Honoured servants of a chief had standing and were still expected to wait. The picture in these ayat used a hierarchy the audience navigated daily.
studies.didYouKnow: The command that closes the message given to every messenger here, an instruction to worship Me in the first person, returns near the end of this surah's gallery of prophets, where the whole community of the messengers is addressed as one and given the identical words. The surah opens and closes its argument about prophecy with the same two-word sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is presented as monotonous in the strict sense: one message, repeated without variation, across every messenger. That removes the possibility of development or negotiation in the content. The correction that follows models something else. It does not deny that the beings in question are exalted; it changes the category from kinship to service, which preserves reverence while relocating it, and leaves the objectors more than they had claimed rather than less.

crossReferences.why: Closes the gallery of prophets in this surah with the same first-person command to worship Me.
States the same universal mission, that a messenger was raised in every community with one instruction.
Addresses the same claim about the angels, asking whether they witnessed their own creation.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the impulse to speak before the person who actually decides has spoken, in a meeting, at home, in a group chat. Hold one comment back today and let the silence sit. The passage describes nearness as including that restraint, which is a strange and useful thing to test in an ordinary room.

studies.title: They Tremble In Awe
studies.meaning: The description continues with three more limits. His knowledge runs before and behind them, their intercession is confined to those He has approved, and they are in awe of Him. Then a conditional is put that seems unnecessary: if any of them were to claim divinity, the outcome is named without hesitation. Commentators read the clause as hypothetical, framed to close a door rather than to report an event, since the point is that no exception exists anywhere in the order.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage completes the surah's answer to those who took intermediaries alongside God, and it is careful to leave the beings themselves honoured. Mecca's practice assumed that nearness to God could be converted into influence with Him, and these lines dismantle that assumption without mocking anyone who held it. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A verb for finding something acceptable and being pleased with it. The condition on intercession is God's approval of the one interceded for, so the whole transaction begins at the far end from the petitioner.
A fear that comes from knowing what something is, rather than from expecting harm. The Quran associates it especially with those who know most, which is why it fits beings described as nearest.
A word for tender anxiety, close to the care a person feels for someone fragile. It occurs twice in this surah, and it describes a fear with concern in it rather than terror.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Intercession in Mecca was a matter of access. A man in trouble found someone close to power and asked him to speak, and the value of a patron was measured by how freely he could be approached. Devotion at the sanctuary worked on the same assumption. These ayat leave the nearness intact and remove the access, which was the part that made the arrangement useful to anyone.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing these beings as apprehensive occurs twice in this surah. Here it is used of those nearest to God, and later it is used of the prophets themselves, who are said to call on Him in longing and in awe. The Quran applies the same trembling to the highest creatures and to its own messengers.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear is presented as a feature of nearness rather than of distance, which reverses the ordinary expectation that familiarity relaxes awe. The limit placed on intercession makes a related point: proximity to God does not translate into leverage over Him. And the hypothetical at the end establishes that the rule holds without exception, so no rank anywhere in creation converts into a claim.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word later in this surah, of prophets calling upon God in longing and in awe.
States the same limit on intercession, that none intercedes with Him except by His leave.
Says it is those who know among His servants who stand in awe of Him.

studies.applyIt: Consider who you would ask to put in a word for you, and notice how naturally the thought forms. Then read the second half of this passage again. Nothing here forbids asking anyone for help. It removes the idea that closeness to God is a channel you can borrow, which changes where you start rather than whether you ask.

studies.title: Sewn Shut, Then Torn Open
studies.meaning: Two claims in one sentence, both offered as things already visible. The heavens and the earth were a single closed mass and were split apart; the commentators record several readings of what that describes, including the separation of sky from earth, and rain released from a closed sky onto ground opened for plants. The second claim is unqualified: every living thing was made from water. The ayah then asks a question rather than concluding.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah that runs through the line of prophets and answers a community demanding proof. This ayah opens a sequence of signs drawn from the physical world: mountains set as stabilisers, the sky as a guarded roof, sun and moon each in an orbit. No specific occasion is reported. The audience were desert people for whom the connection between water and life needed no argument at all.

keyTerms.note: A word for a tear that has been mended, or cloth with no opening in it. It describes a state of being sealed rather than merely joined, which is why the verb that answers it is one of tearing.
The exact opposite of the previous word, from the same domain of cloth and stitching. The pairing is deliberate and the translation cannot hold it: one word closes the seam and the next opens it.
The plain adjective for alive, attached to every thing without qualification. The construction covers plants, animals and people in one phrase, which is what makes the claim as wide as it is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water in Arabia was the whole economy compressed into one substance. Wells were owned, fought over and named; a settlement existed because of one and vanished when it failed. Wealth was measured in access to it, and a caravan route was a chain of watering points. Telling that audience every living thing was made from water was not introducing a new idea. It was giving a familiar dependence a first cause.
studies.didYouKnow: The two key words are opposites built for each other, and both come from the vocabulary of sewing. The ayah is also addressed to those who reject the message and asks whether they have not seen, which assumes the evidence is already in front of them. Nothing is being revealed here; the argument is that they are being asked to notice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument runs from the structure of the world to a single maker, and it does so without claiming to describe how. The commentators kept several readings open rather than settling one, which is itself instructive: the ayah is making a claim about origin and dependence, not delivering an account of mechanism. What is asserted is that things now separate were once one, and that life is not self-standing but is drawn from something given.

crossReferences.why: Describes the heaven as smoke before it was ordered into seven.
Extends the water claim: God created every moving creature from water.
Water sent down raises gardens and grain, and is called the coming out.

studies.applyIt: Drink a glass of water today slowly enough to finish the thought that you are made mostly of it. That is all. The ayah works by asking whether people have looked, and the fastest way to test it is to take the most ordinary thing you will touch today and give it fifteen seconds of actual attention.

studies.title: Each Floating In An Orbit
studies.meaning: Three features of the world are named and each is given a purpose. Mountains are set as anchors so the ground does not lurch underfoot, and openings are cut through them so people can find their way. The sky is called a guarded roof, and the complaint attached is that its signs are passed over. Then night, day, sun and moon are gathered into one sentence, and all of them are said to be swimming, each in its own course.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been arguing that the world is not a plaything and that its ordering points somewhere. This passage supplies the evidence, drawn from what any listener could verify by looking down at the ground and up at the sky. Navigation by both was ordinary skill in Arabia. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these three ayat.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a ship dropping anchor and holding fast. The word is not the ordinary term for a mountain; it names them by the function this ayah gives them, which is steadying.
Broad openings between heights, the gaps a traveller actually uses. The word occurs twice in the Quran and both times it describes the earth as arranged so that people can move through it.
A verb for moving freely through a medium. The same word appears thirteen ayat earlier in this surah for those near God glorifying Him, so one motion covers worship and orbit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian travel depended on both halves of this ayah. Routes ran through named passes between the western hills, and a guide's knowledge was a list of those gaps in order. At night the same journey was navigated by stars, whose risings and settings were memorised as a calendar for rain, harvest and raiding. The audience did not admire the sky. They used it, every clear night of the year.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for the sun and moon moving in their courses is the same verb the surah used thirteen ayat earlier for those near God glorifying Him. Arabic builds its word for glorification on the image of swimming, so the Quran describes worship and celestial motion with one root, and this surah places both uses within a page of each other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Each thing named is described by what it does for someone. The mountains steady, the passes guide, the sky protects, the lights move in fixed courses. That turns the natural order into a set of provisions rather than a set of facts, and it makes inattention the specific failure the passage names. Nothing here argues that the world proves God. It argues that the world is arranged, and that people are looking past the arrangement.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb thirteen ayat earlier, there of continuous glorification by those near God.
Describes the same courses, with sun and moon each swimming in an orbit and neither overtaking the other.
Uses the same word for wide passes, saying the earth was spread so people could travel its roads.

studies.applyIt: Go outside after dark this week and find the moon, then work out roughly where it was a week ago. Two minutes is enough. The ayah's charge is not disbelief but turning away from signs, and the cheapest correction available is to look up once on purpose rather than never.

studies.title: Every Soul Tastes Death
studies.meaning: The first ayah answers opponents who were waiting for the messenger to die, and the answer is a question: no human being before him was given permanence, so would they be the ones to last. Then the statement widens to everyone. Death is described with a verb of tasting, which makes it an experience passed through rather than an ending. And the test is said to come in two forms, hardship and good, with both named as trial.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators report that opponents in Mecca were saying openly that they had only to wait for the man to die and the matter would end, and read the first ayah as answering that calculation. The reports are widely transmitted though the wording varies. The surah belongs to the middle Meccan period, when the message had a following small enough for its opponents to think in those terms.

keyTerms.note: The noun for remaining without end, used elsewhere of the garden and the fire. Denying it to every human being before the messenger places him in the same category as everyone he is addressing.

An active participle from the verb to taste, which implies a brief and direct experience rather than a permanent state. The choice makes death something the soul goes through, and the grammar of the phrase leaves nobody out.
Placed at the end of the clause to cover both terms before it. Hardship and prosperity are named as one thing rather than two, and the word's root is the fire used to test metal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Waiting out an opponent was a real political strategy in a society organised by clans and lifetimes. A leader's death dissolved his following, and a claim died with the man who made it unless sons or a sworn group carried it. Meccan opponents had watched movements collapse that way before. The question the ayah puts back to them is the one that arrangement never considered: what happens to the people doing the waiting.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about every soul tasting death appears three times in the Quran, each time followed by something different: here by the two-sided test, elsewhere by wages paid in full on the Day, and elsewhere by a plain statement that you will be returned to God. The repetition with varied continuations is one of the ways the Quran turns a single line into several arguments.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming prosperity as a test alongside hardship is the ayah's sharp edge. Most people treat difficulty as the thing to be endured and ease as the reward, and this sentence puts them on the same footing. That changes what a good period is for. It also removes the last argument for treating any human being as permanent, including the one delivering the message, which the surah has just spent many ayat establishing about earlier prophets.

crossReferences.why: The same sentence, followed there by wages paid in full on the Day.
Answers the same calculation directly after a battle in which the report spread.
Shows the two-sided test from the inside, honour read as favour and hardship as slight.

studies.applyIt: Think about the best month you have had in the last five years. Then ask what you did with it, in the same tone you would ask what you did with the worst month. The ayah puts prosperity and hardship in one sentence as a single test, and most people have never audited the good half.

studies.title: Is This The One
studies.meaning: The ayah turns on one word used twice. He is mocked for mentioning their gods, and in the same breath they reject the mention of the Merciful. Commentators note the asymmetry: they defend objects they only inherited, and dismiss the name that is not theirs to defend. The ridicule itself is described as their whole manner of receiving him, and the question they ask each other is designed to be answered by a laugh rather than by a reply.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Ridicule rather than argument is the response reported through this stretch of the surah, and other passages of the period record the same tactic. The name the Merciful was itself contested in Mecca, where some objected to it as unfamiliar, so the closing clause names a real point of resistance. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: Not the act of mocking but the thing mocked. The grammar makes him into a category of joke, which is a different and colder posture than disagreement.
The verb behind the Quran's word for remembrance. The ayah uses its noun again at the end, so mentioning their gods and the mention of the Merciful are described with one root.
A name whose form suggests an overwhelming and general mercy. Several passages record Meccan resistance to this particular name, which is why the ayah closes on it rather than on the word for God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a weapon with a known edge in Arabia. Satirical verse could destroy a man's standing across the peninsula in a season, and tribes retained poets partly for that purpose. A joke repeated at the gatherings around the sanctuary travelled with the caravans. Being made into a figure of ridicule was not a private humiliation; it was a coordinated method of removing someone from serious consideration.
studies.didYouKnow: One Arabic root carries the whole ayah. He is faulted for mentioning their gods, and the same root returns at the end as the mention of the Merciful that they reject. The Quran's word for remembrance comes from that root, so an accusation and the thing being refused are named with the same vocabulary in a single line.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows how devotion can attach itself to what a person merely inherited while rejecting what actually addresses them. It also records something about ridicule: it is a way of declining to have the conversation, and the Quran answers it by describing it rather than by returning it. What is being defended in the ayah is not an argument but a name, and names are what the surah keeps returning to.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same mockery in almost the same words, asking whether this is the one God sent as a messenger.
Records resistance to this name directly, with people asking what the Merciful is when told to prostrate.
Answers this mockery five ayat later, saying messengers before him were ridiculed too.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you defend automatically because it is yours, and what you dismiss because it arrived from outside. Pick one opinion you hold in each category today and swap the treatment for five minutes: question the inherited one, and take the outside one seriously. The ayah is describing a habit, not a doctrine.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Created Out Of Haste
studies.meaning: A statement about human nature is made in four words, and it is stronger than saying people are impatient. The human being is described as made from haste, as though hurry were the material rather than the habit. Commentators offer that reading and also a milder one, that the expression is an intensification. The instruction that follows is not to slow down in general but not to press for the signs, and the next line shows exactly the pressing that was meant.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Demands to see the threatened outcome immediately are reported repeatedly through this period, sometimes as genuine challenge and sometimes as taunt. The community itself was also waiting, under pressure and without relief, so the instruction lands on both sides of the argument. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these two ayat, which continue the exchange begun with the mockery a line earlier.

keyTerms.note: This phrasing, made from haste, occurs only here. Arabic can use the preposition for material, as clay or dust, which is why the classical readings differ over how literally to take it.
A promise in the first person with the future prefix attached. The signs are not withheld, only timed, which is the whole distinction the ayah is drawing between refusal and delay.
One word for a promise of good and of harm alike. The questioners use it here for the outcome they doubt, and the surah returns to it near the end when it is said to have drawn near.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Waiting was structural in Arabia and nobody enjoyed it. A caravan's return was expected within a window of weeks, not days; a debt fell due at a named season; rain came or did not and the answer arrived months after the sowing. Everything important was slow and uncertain. That is precisely why demanding immediate proof was a familiar and effective way to embarrass a claim.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrasing here, that the human being was created from haste, occurs only once in the Quran. Arabic uses the same construction elsewhere for the material something is made of, clay in one place and a drop in another, which is why the classical commentators had to decide whether this is a statement about substance or a figure of speech. They record both readings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats impatience as a fact about human beings rather than as a fault to be scolded, and then places a single limit on it. What may not be hurried is God's own schedule. That distinction matters: the ayah does not ask for calm or resignation, and it does not defend the delay. It simply refuses to let the timing of the signs be set by the people demanding them.

crossReferences.why: States the same trait plainly, that the human being prays for evil as he prays for good, being hasty.
Answers the same demand, saying the command of God is coming, so do not seek to hurry it.
Returns to the promise at the end of this surah, where it is described as having drawn near.

studies.applyIt: Catch one moment of hurry today that has nothing behind it: refreshing a screen, checking whether they have replied, opening the same app twice. Let it pass without acting once. The ayah does not ask you to become patient. It asks you to notice that hurry is what you are made of, which is easier to see in something trivial.

studies.title: If They Only Knew
studies.meaning: The sentence is deliberately unfinished. If they knew the moment when they cannot keep the fire off their faces or their backs, then what follows is never said, and Arabic allows that ending because the listener supplies it. What is described in the gap is oddly domestic: hands trying to shield a face, and failing. Front and back are both named, which closes off the ordinary human response of turning away from what is coming.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage answers the demand made a line earlier for the promised outcome to arrive now. The surah does not give a date; it describes the condition instead. Its listeners had just been told they were made of haste, and this is what the thing they were hurrying towards is said to look like. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A conditional whose consequence is left unstated, a recognised device in Arabic. Withholding the answer makes the sentence heavier than any completion would, since the listener finishes it privately.
A verb for restraining or keeping something away with the hand. It belongs to ordinary defensive gesture, which is what makes the failure described here physical rather than abstract.
The passive of a verb for coming to someone's aid in a fight. It closes the ayah by removing the last resort of a threatened man in that society, which was that someone else would arrive.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Help in Arabia meant kinsmen. A man under attack shouted the name of his clan and expected men to come, and the entire security of life rested on that expectation being reliable. Someone with no one to call was already effectively dead. The final clause of this ayah, that they will not be helped, described the most frightening condition the audience could imagine before it described anything else.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah is grammatically incomplete. Arabic permits a conditional to be left without its answer when the answer would be overwhelming, and the classical commentators identify this as one of the clearest examples in the Quran. Several supply the missing clause in their commentaries, and they do not agree on it, precisely because the text declines to say.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Warning is delivered here as a gap rather than as a description, which respects the listener more than a catalogue would. The detail that is given is chosen carefully: not the fire's heat but the failure of a reflex, the hand that cannot cover the face. That locates the horror in helplessness rather than in pain, and it answers the demand of the previous ayah by suggesting that knowing would not be a favour.

crossReferences.why: Completes the picture in the next line, saying it will come suddenly and leave them stunned.
Gives a similar physical detail, garments of tar and the fire covering their faces.
Describes the fire scorching their faces, another image of the face as what cannot be shielded.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you do with a thought you would rather not finish. The ayah leaves its own sentence hanging on purpose, and most people do the same with anything serious. Pick one thing you have been leaving unfinished in your head and complete it, in writing, in a single sentence today. Then put it down and carry on.

studies.title: It Will Come Suddenly
studies.meaning: The unfinished sentence before this one is answered with a correction: not only will they be unable to shield themselves, it will not even announce itself. The verb chosen means to strike someone dumb, to leave them without a reply, and it occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Two abilities are then denied in order. They cannot turn it back, and they are not given the pause that a condemned man in that world could sometimes negotiate.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah closes the surah's answer to those who asked when the promise would arrive. Suddenness is the standing reply in passages of this period, since a dated threat would allow preparation at the last moment and would turn the whole matter into a calculation. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: An adverb the Quran uses repeatedly for how the hour and the punishment arrive. It denies not the certainty but the schedule, which is what every questioner in this surah has been asking for.
This verb occurs only here. Its root describes being struck speechless by something overwhelming, and it gives Arabic the word for a slander that leaves the accused with nothing to say.
From a root for looking and waiting, used of a creditor granting more time. Denying it removes the negotiation that ordinarily follows a verdict in a society without prisons.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Respite was the normal currency of Arabian justice. A blood claim could be settled with time to gather camels, a debtor could be granted another season, and a condemned man's clan could buy delay while they negotiated. Almost nothing was final at the moment it was pronounced. An outcome that arrives with no interval and no possibility of arrangement described something outside the audience's entire experience of consequence.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for being struck dumb occurs only once in the Quran. Its root supplies the ordinary Arabic word for a false accusation, because such a charge leaves its target speechless, and the same root appears in the account of a king struck dumb when Abraham turned an argument against him. One root covers both kinds of silence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Suddenness is doing theological work here, not dramatic work. A dated end would permit a strategy, and the whole point of the surah's argument is that there is no strategy available, only a manner of living. The removal of respite makes the same claim from the other side. What is being described is not cruelty but the closing of the gap in which people habitually plan to make their arrangements later.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same root when a king is left speechless after Abraham turns his own argument against him.
Says the hour will not come upon them except suddenly, in answer to the same question about its timing.
Urges following the best of what was revealed before the punishment arrives suddenly and unperceived.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you are planning to sort out when you have more warning: a conversation, an apology, a medical appointment. Do the smallest possible piece of it today, in under ten minutes. The ayah's argument is not that you should be afraid. It is that the interval you are counting on is not yours to count on.

studies.title: Who Guards You By Night
studies.meaning: Two answers to the ridicule reported earlier. The first is historical: messengers before him were mocked, and what closed in on the mockers was the very thing they had made a joke of. The second is a question with no available reply. Who keeps watch over you, night and day, against the Merciful. Commentators note the name chosen, since the question would land differently with any other. The line ends by reporting that they turn from the mention of their Lord.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The community was small and mocked, and the reassurance offered is not that the mockery will stop but that it has a precedent and an outcome. The question that follows addresses an audience who believed in God and relied on other protections alongside Him, which is why it asks about guarding rather than about existence. No specific occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for something encircling and then descending on a person. The Quran uses it almost exclusively of a consequence returning to whoever set it in motion, which is exactly the shape of this sentence.

keyTerms.gloss: guards you, keeps watch over you
keyTerms.note: This verb occurs only here. It is the word for a night watchman minding sleeping people or grazing animals, so the question is about who is awake while you are not.

The word that closed the surah's first ayah, returning for the third time in this stretch. It marks the same posture throughout: not argument against the message but a body turned in another direction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every camp posted a watch. Someone stayed awake over the animals and the sleeping tents, because a raid came before dawn or not at all, and a man who dozed cost the party its herd. Payment, rotation and the reliability of particular watchmen were ordinary subjects of conversation. Asking who keeps watch over you by night used the most familiar arrangement in Arabian life to ask an unfamiliar question.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for keeping watch in the second of these ayat occurs only once in the whole Quran. It belongs to the vocabulary of herding and guarding, and Arabic still uses its noun for a guardian or protector. The Quran asks its most searching question about dependence using a word borrowed from the night shift over a flock.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The first ayah reframes mockery as something with a history and a direction, which removes its power to isolate. The second makes a claim about dependence: whatever else guards a person, it is not what they would need guarding from. That closes the space in which other protectors are imagined to operate, and it does so by asking rather than asserting, leaving the listener to notice that there is no name to supply.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same statement about earlier messengers being mocked and the mockery closing in on the mockers.
Reports the ridicule five ayat earlier that these two lines are answering.
Asks the same kind of question, who is an army for you or who would provide if He withheld.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, before you sleep, name the arrangements you are relying on to keep you safe: a lock, insurance, a job, a person who would answer the phone. Then read the question in this ayah again. You are not being asked to give any of them up, only to notice what they cover and what they do not.

studies.title: Until Their Lives Grew Long
studies.meaning: A possible answer to the previous question is raised and dismissed in one line: gods who could defend them cannot even help themselves. Then the real explanation for their confidence is given, and it is not an argument. They and their fathers were given enjoyment until a long life made the arrangement seem permanent. Against that, one observation is offered about land being reduced at its edges, and one question. Are they then the ones who prevail.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience were the leading families of a city whose prosperity had run for generations, and the surah names duration itself as the source of their assurance. The remark about land diminishing at its edges is read by commentators in more than one way, including as territory passing out of the control of those who held it, and they record the range. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: This passive occurs only here. It comes from the word for a companion, and Arabic uses it for the protection a travelling companion owes, so what is denied is escort as much as defence.
A verb for granting the use of something for a period. It carries a term inside it: what is given this way is on loan, which is exactly what a long run of good fortune makes easy to forget.
The outer parts of something. Commentators read the diminishing at the edges as land or people passing out of their control, and the classical works record several explanations without deciding.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan confidence rested on a run of decades. Two caravans a year, custodianship of the sanctuary, and treaties with tribes along the routes had produced a stability nobody living could remember being without. Wealth arrived on a schedule. In a peninsula where most groups lived season to season, a city where the pattern had held for three generations felt to its people like a permanent arrangement rather than a lucky one.
studies.didYouKnow: The observation about land being diminished at its edges appears twice in the Quran, here and in one other surah, in nearly identical words. Both times it is introduced with the same phrase, do they not see, so it is offered as something already visible rather than as a prediction. The classical commentaries record several readings of what the shrinking describes and settle on none.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies duration as the thing that produces false confidence, which is a precise observation about how people actually come to believe they are secure. Nothing was argued to them; a long stretch of comfort did the work. Against that, the answer offered is not a threat but an invitation to look at a trend already underway, and to ask whether the run they are inside is the same thing as an outcome.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same observation about the earth being diminished at its edges, adding that nothing reverses His judgement.
Asks the question this ayah answers, about who guards them by night and day.
Describes towns that exulted in their means, whose dwellings were scarcely inhabited afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Ask what in your life feels permanent only because it has lasted a while: an income, a health, an arrangement at home. Name one out loud today and add the word so far. Not as a warning to yourself. Just as an accurate description, which is what this passage says the long run makes people stop giving.

studies.title: A Single Breath Of It
studies.meaning: The role is defined narrowly. He warns, and the warning is by revelation, which means he adds nothing of his own and guarantees no result. Then the difficulty is stated as a fact about hearing rather than about willingness: the deaf do not hear a call, even when it is a warning. The second ayah measures what would be enough. Not the punishment but a breath of it, the faintest touch, and the confession arrives immediately and in full.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been reporting mockery and demands for proof, and these two ayat close that exchange by describing the limits of what a messenger does. The tension in the Meccan years between visible failure and continued warning runs through many passages of this period. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these two ayat.

keyTerms.note: The word for what is conveyed swiftly and privately. Placing it here limits the warner's claim: what he transmits is not his assessment of the situation but what was given to him.
Used of an inability rather than a refusal, which makes the image sharper than calling them stubborn. A deaf man is not disobeying the call; the call simply does not reach him.
This word occurs only here in the Quran. It names the lightest passing touch of air, as a scent reaches you, and it is chosen to measure how little would be required.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scent carried information in Arabia. A traveller smelled water before he saw it, smoke told him a camp lay ahead, and perfume announced a person's arrival in a room. The word used here belongs to that world of things detected on the air before they are seen. Saying a mere breath of the punishment would be enough measured it in the smallest unit the language had.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for a breath of the punishment occurs only once in the Quran. Its root is the one Arabic uses for scent carried on moving air, and it is deliberately the lightest possible measure. The confession that follows it, that they were wrongdoers, is word for word the same admission made by a destroyed town earlier in this surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two limits are set side by side. A messenger cannot make anyone hear, and the smallest touch of consequence makes everyone speak. Between those two facts lies the whole difficulty of warning: what would produce the response is exactly what the warning exists to prevent. The passage does not resolve that, and it does not make the messenger responsible for it. His task is stated in one clause and stops there.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical confession in the mouths of a town earlier in this surah, at the moment of destruction.
Repeats that you cannot make the deaf hear the call when they turn away in retreat.
States the same limit on the role, that he is a reminder and not one to compel them.

studies.applyIt: If you have been trying to convince someone of something important and getting nowhere, take this ayah as permission. Say it once more, plainly, and then stop managing the outcome. The passage assigns you the warning and gives you no responsibility for the hearing, which is a lighter load than most people carry.

studies.title: The Weight Of A Mustard Seed
studies.meaning: Scales are set up, and the word for them is plural while the word for justice stands alone beside it, which commentators read as saying the balances themselves simply are justice rather than being calibrated to it. Then the guarantee is made concrete in the smallest unit anyone could picture. Even the weight of a mustard seed is brought and produced. The closing phrase is unexpectedly plain: We are sufficient as reckoners, with no threat attached.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just described people who confess only when a breath of consequence touches them, and this ayah supplies what they will actually meet. Weights and balances were the everyday instruments of a trading city, and disputes about them were common enough that the image needed no explanation. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: A plural, and this definite form occurs only here. Commentators differ over whether the plural means many scales or the many things weighed, and the classical works record both without deciding.

A word for giving each party its precise due, used in commerce for correct measure. Placed beside the scales without a connecting word, it makes justice the nature of the instrument rather than its setting.
The mustard seed was the proverbial smallest thing in the region, familiar from cooking and medicine. The Quran uses it twice, both times to make a point about nothing being too small to be located.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on weights. Gold and silver were measured rather than counted, spices and incense were sold by fractions of a unit, and every serious transaction involved a balance whose accuracy someone could dispute. Merchants carried their own weights. A promise that the scales at the end would be exact spoke to people who spent their working lives watching a beam settle and arguing about where it stopped.
studies.didYouKnow: The mustard seed appears twice in the Quran. Here it measures what will be brought to the scales, and in the other place it is spoken by a father advising his son, saying that even that weight, hidden in a rock or anywhere in the heavens or the earth, will be brought out. Both passages use the smallest unit their audience could picture.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The guarantee runs in the direction people rarely expect. The ayah does not promise that nothing small will be missed in punishment; it promises that no soul will be wronged, and the seed is brought precisely so that nothing owed is lost. That makes exactness a mercy rather than a threat. The closing phrase reinforces it, since a reckoner who is sufficient needs no witnesses, no advocates and no records but His own.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same mustard seed, promising that even hidden in a rock God will bring it out.
States the same guarantee, that God does not wrong by the weight of the smallest particle.
Closes a short surah with the same principle, an atom's weight of good or evil being seen.

studies.applyIt: Think of one small good you did that nobody noticed, and one small unfairness you suffered that was never acknowledged. Hold both for a moment against the promise in this ayah. You are not being asked to stop minding. You are being told that the record you assumed was lost is being kept to a finer resolution than you would have asked for.

studies.title: A Blessed Reminder Sent Down
studies.meaning: The gallery of prophets opens with what was given rather than with what happened. Moses and Aaron received three things: a criterion that separates, a light, and a reminder for those who guard themselves. Those people are then described by two marks, fearing their Lord where no one sees and being anxious about the hour. The passage turns without transition to the present book, calls it blessed, and asks a question. Then Abraham is introduced by what he was given.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has finished arguing and now begins its sequence of prophets, and it starts by putting the present revelation in the same category as the earlier ones. Meccan objections often treated the Quran as unprecedented; describing it in the vocabulary already used for what Moses received answers that directly. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: From a root for splitting apart. The Quran uses this name six times, twice of what was given to Moses and elsewhere of its own function, so it describes a book by what it distinguishes.
Read two ways by the commentators: fearing a Lord they cannot see, or fearing Him where others cannot see them. The classical works keep both, and the ayah supports either.
A word for maturity of discernment, the quality that lets someone be trusted with his own affairs. Attached to Abraham with a possessive, it names something given to him in particular.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being trusted with your own property marked the end of youth in Arabia. A young man's inheritance stayed under guardianship until he showed the settled judgement to handle it, and the assessment was made by relatives who watched how he dealt with animals, debts and disputes. The word used for what Abraham was given is the word for passing that test, which is why the ayah adds that God knew him.
studies.didYouKnow: The name used here for what Moses and Aaron received, the criterion, is used six times in the Quran. Two of those describe what was given to Moses, one is the title of an entire surah, and the rest describe the present revelation or a day of decisive separation. One word links the two books the surah has just placed side by side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes continuity its argument. What was given before is described in three terms, and the present book is then placed in the same series, with the question left as a question. The description of the people it benefits is equally deliberate: they are marked by fear in private and unease about a day nobody has seen, which are qualities invisible to any observer and therefore impossible to perform.

crossReferences.why: Records the same gift to Moses, the book and the criterion, so that they might be guided.
Uses the same name for the present revelation, sent down to be a warner to all the worlds.
Continues immediately, showing what the judgement given to Abraham looked like when he used it.

studies.applyIt: The people this book benefits are described by something no one can see. Pick one small act this week that nobody will know about: a debt settled quietly, a message of thanks sent and not mentioned, a fast nobody is told of. The point is not the act. It is having one thing in your life that is not being performed for anybody.

studies.title: What Are These Statues
studies.meaning: The confrontation begins with a question about an object, not a doctrine. He asks what these figures are, and the word he uses is the plain one for carved likenesses rather than any religious term. The answer given is not a defence of the statues at all: we found our fathers doing this. He replies by including the fathers in the verdict, which is the part that stings. Their response is to ask whether he is serious or playing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience lived beside a sanctuary filled with such objects, and the argument from ancestral practice was the standing Meccan reply to the message. Placing that exact exchange in Abraham's mouth was pointed, since Quraysh traced their own custodianship of the sanctuary back to him. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: From a root for resemblance. The word names them as images of something rather than as gods, which settles the question grammatically before the argument starts.
Remaining beside something in attachment. The Quran uses the same word for those who keep to the Sacred House and for people found attending idols, so the posture is neutral and the object decides.
A verb of discovery, not of choice. The answer describes inherited practice as something encountered rather than adopted, which is exactly why the reply that follows extends the verdict backwards.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ancestral practice was the strongest argument available in Arabia. Lineage was memorised, a man's standing came from his fathers, and departing from what they had done was closer to disloyalty than to error. The sanctuary's arrangements were maintained by families who had inherited specific roles in them. Asking a Meccan to judge his fathers mistaken was asking him to give up the ground he stood on.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Abraham uses for the statues occurs only twice in the Quran. The other place describes objects made for Solomon by those working under him, alongside basins and cauldrons, and there the word carries no reproach at all. The Quran's objection in this passage is to what people do beside such things, not to the craft of making them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exchange isolates the real argument, which is never about the objects. Nobody in it defends the statues; the defence offered is continuity with the fathers, and the reply refuses to treat inheritance as evidence. That is a heavy thing to say in any society. The final question is equally revealing: faced with a claim they cannot answer, they ask whether it is a joke, which is the same move the surah reported at its opening.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for playing earlier in this surah, where creation is denied as a diversion.
