Gives the same answer from the fathers, and reports that every warned town replied in exactly those terms.
Narrates the same conversation at greater length, ending with Abraham naming the Lord of the worlds.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing you do because it was done in your family, and ask what it is for. Some answers will be good, and you will hold the practice more firmly for having asked. Some will not, and you can decide separately what to do about that. The ayah's objection is to the answer, not to the inheritance.

studies.title: The One Who Originated Them
studies.meaning: The answer to the question about whether he is joking is a correction, not a defence. He does not say he is serious; he supplies what they asked for and replaces their object with a claim about origin. The verb chosen describes splitting something open to bring it into being, which is a specific picture rather than a general word for making. Then he adds a line nobody required of him: he is among the witnesses to that.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Abraham's confrontation is being told to an audience who traced their sanctuary to him and who had just been described as answering the message with the same combination of inherited practice and mockery. The reply given here matches the surah's own method, which is to argue from what made the world rather than from what was inherited. No specific occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a root for splitting or cleaving open, used of dough breaking and of a first opening. It describes creation as bringing something out that was not there, rather than as arranging what was.
A particle that cancels what came before and substitutes a correction. Abraham begins his answer with it, so the sentence sets aside their question rather than answering it on their terms.
The word for a legal witness who testifies to what he knows. Adding himself to that class turns a statement about God into personal testimony that can be held against him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the load-bearing institution of Arabian life. Contracts, marriages, debts and blood settlements held because named men had witnessed them and would say so, and a witness who was found unreliable lost standing permanently. Declaring yourself a witness was therefore a costly move, not a rhetorical one. Abraham attaching himself to the claim placed his own credit behind it in front of everyone present.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb Abraham uses for originating the heavens and the earth gives Arabic its word for breaking a fast, because both come from the sense of splitting something open or breaking through. The same root supplies the Quran's word for the original disposition a person is made with, so one root covers a first creation, a first nature, and a first meal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply relocates the argument from objects to origin, which is where it has to go, since nobody disputes that a statue exists. It also shows what belief looks like when it becomes testimony. Abraham does not merely hold a view; he places himself in the position of a witness, which is a claim other people are entitled to test. That move is the whole difference between an opinion and a stand.

crossReferences.why: Gives Abraham's parallel declaration, that he turns his face to the One who originated the heavens and earth.
Uses the same root for the original nature God made people upon, with no altering of it.
Opens a surah with the same divine name, the Originator of the heavens and the earth.

studies.applyIt: Say one thing you believe out loud today to someone who might disagree, plainly and without a joke attached to soften it. Not an argument. Just the statement, once. This ayah's second half is what distinguishes holding a view privately from standing behind it, and the difference is felt rather than reasoned.

studies.title: Except The Biggest Of Them
studies.meaning: An oath is sworn and a plan announced in advance, to be carried out once the people have gone. What follows is precise: everything is broken into fragments except the largest, and a reason is attached, so that they might come back to it. Commentators read the exception as the whole point, since a demonstration needs a survivor to be questioned. The search that follows produces a witness who remembers hearing a young man speak about the objects.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The account belongs to Abraham's early confrontation with his community, and this surah gives it in more detail than any other. The audience in Mecca maintained objects at a sanctuary and were themselves being addressed by a man whose speech about those objects was already public knowledge. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a plan made quietly against something. It is normally used of the opponents of prophets, and the Quran allows Abraham the same word, applied to objects rather than to people.
This word occurs only here in the Quran. It names debris small enough that nothing can be reassembled, which is what makes the single untouched figure conspicuous.
The word for a young man in his strength, used elsewhere of a servant travelling with a prophet. It records how he was known in the town: by age and by talk, not by any position.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Damage to communal property was a serious matter in any Arabian settlement, and the first move was always the same: find who was heard saying something beforehand. Reputations travelled through overheard talk at wells and markets, and a young man with unusual opinions would be known by everyone without being important to anyone. The investigation in these ayat follows the procedure the audience would have expected.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the broken fragments occurs only once in the whole Quran. The word describing Abraham as a youth occurs four times, and the others are a servant in the household of Egypt and the young companion who travels with Moses in a later surah. In each case the term marks someone young enough to be spoken about rather than consulted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records a prophet acting rather than only arguing, and it shows the act designed as an argument. The exception left standing is the reasoning made physical: the case will be won by what the survivors cannot do, not by what Abraham says. There is also honesty in the announcement of the plan beforehand, which the Quran preserves. Nothing here is done secretly except the timing.

crossReferences.why: Narrates the same episode, with Abraham addressing the offerings before turning on the figures.
Delivers the point of the exception three ayat later, when he tells them to ask the biggest one.
Uses the same word for a youth, of the young companion travelling with Moses on a journey.

studies.applyIt: Notice that Abraham did not argue the point, he arranged for the argument to make itself. If you are trying to convince someone of something, ask whether there is a small thing you could set up that would let them see it, instead of another explanation. People believe what they work out. That is the method this passage records.

studies.title: They Returned To Themselves
studies.meaning: A public hearing is arranged, and the answer given there is famous for being obviously untrue. He attributes the act to the largest figure and tells them to ask the others if they can speak, which places the whole case on that single condition. Commentators note that the statement is a challenge shaped like a claim, not a lie meant to be believed. The result is described in one phrase: they went back to themselves, and turned the accusation inward.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The scene is staged deliberately, since the leaders themselves call for the trial to be held in front of the crowd. That detail matters for a Meccan audience whose own leaders had held quiet conferences about how to respond to the message, reported at the opening of this surah. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these four ayat.

keyTerms.note: An idiom for a fully public setting. The leaders choose it to make the case decisive, which is the same choice that then makes their own reversal happen in front of everyone.
A verb for producing articulate speech. It occurs twice in this surah, once in Abraham's condition and once in their answer, so the case turns on a single word used by both sides.
The ordinary verb for going back, here directed at themselves. Arabic can express reflection as a physical return, so the moment of realisation is described as walking back into your own house.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public hearings were how Arabian communities settled accusations. The parties spoke before an assembly, reputations were made and lost in the exchange, and there was no appeal beyond what the gathering concluded. A man who lost such an exchange lost more than the case. That is why calling the crowd was a confident move by the leaders, and why the reversal recorded here would have been so costly to them.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for speaking that carries the whole argument appears twice in this surah, in Abraham's condition and in the reply he draws out of them. Their answer, that these do not speak, is the concession he was after, and it is given by the prosecution rather than argued by the defence. The case is decided by a sentence the other side volunteers.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates conviction in a moment nobody engineered. They return to themselves, and what they find there they say out loud before they can manage it. That suggests a knowledge already present, needing only to be uncovered rather than supplied. The staging matters too. Truth here does not arrive as information; it arrives when a question is put in a form that cannot be answered without conceding.

crossReferences.why: Shows the recognition collapsing in the next line, as they are turned back on their heads.
Another case decided by a piece of evidence that forces the parties to concede without argument.
Describes rejection that persists although their own selves were convinced of the truth.

studies.applyIt: Think of a moment when you knew you were wrong before you admitted it, and how long the gap was. That gap is what this passage is describing. Next time you feel it opening, say the true thing while it is still uncomfortable, because the ayah after this one shows what happens when the moment is allowed to pass.

studies.title: Turned Back On Their Heads
studies.meaning: The recognition lasts one line. They are described as being set back on their heads, an image of something inverted, and what comes out is a fact stated as a rebuke: you know perfectly well these do not speak. That sentence concedes everything and is offered as a defence. Abraham's reply does not press the contradiction. He asks instead what such things are for, in terms of benefit and harm, and ends with an exclamation rather than an argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The exchange completes Abraham's confrontation and immediately precedes the decision to burn him. Its Meccan listeners had themselves been told, a few ayat earlier, that the objects they maintained could not defend anyone. The argument is put in a form that requires no scripture and no shared authority, only an admission the other side has already made. No specific occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: This verb occurs only here. It describes something inverted so that its top is at the bottom, and the Quran applies it to a change of mind rather than to a physical posture.

The test offered is capacity, not doctrine. Benefit and harm are the two things anyone can check about anything, which is why the question can be asked of people who share no premises with the questioner.
An interjection rather than a word, occurring three times in the Quran. Elsewhere it names the sound a person must not make to ageing parents, which shows how sharp it was understood to be.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Benefit and harm were how Arabians assessed everything, from a well to an alliance to a marriage. A thing that could neither help you nor hurt you was, in the plainest sense, not a factor. The question put here therefore used the ordinary standard of judgement in that society. What made it uncomfortable was not its difficulty but the fact that nobody had ever applied it to the sanctuary.
studies.didYouKnow: The exclamation Abraham makes occurs three times in the Quran. In one of those places it is the very sound a person is told not to make towards an ageing mother or father, which is how the Quran indicates the limit of what may be said to them. The same syllable marks the sharpest disgust and the smallest forbidden rudeness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows knowledge and conduct coming apart. They have said the decisive thing themselves, and it changes nothing, which suggests that what holds a practice in place is not a belief that could be corrected. Abraham's shift is instructive: having won the argument, he stops arguing and appeals to sense. The final question is not rhetorical, and the passage does not report an answer to it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same exclamation as the limit of what may be said to ageing parents.
Gives the admission in the line before, which this passage shows collapsing almost immediately.
Puts the same test as a parable, that all of them together could not create a fly.

studies.applyIt: Ask the passage's question about one thing you spend real time on: can it actually benefit you, and can it harm you. Answer honestly, in both directions. Some things will pass and you can stop feeling uneasy about them. Some will fail on both counts, and knowing that is not the same as being ready to drop them.

studies.title: Be Coolness And Safety
studies.meaning: The scene is given in four sentences with nothing between them. A crowd decides on burning and calls it support for their gods. God addresses the fire directly, by name, and gives it two attributes: coolness and peace. The commentators note the second word, since cold alone would have been its own harm. Their scheme is turned back on them, and the passage ends with a departure to a land described as blessed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The episode belongs to Abraham's confrontation with his people over the idols he had broken, told at greater length in the ayat before this. No occasion is reported for the passage itself. Its point of contact with the audience was direct: a man who rejected his community's gods and whose community tried to destroy him for it, told to people watching the same pattern begin in their own town.

keyTerms.note: The plain noun for cold, not a verb of extinguishing. The fire is not put out; it is given a different property, which is why the commentators speak of the fire remaining and its harm being removed.

The second attribute is the necessary one. Cold without it would have injured him just as surely, and the classical commentaries make exactly this observation, that the word keeps the rescue from becoming another danger.

A word for a plan made quietly against someone, with the implication of cunning rather than force. Using it of a public burning keeps the emphasis on the intention behind the act rather than on the act, which is what the next clause overturns.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fire was the community's instrument as well as its comfort. Gathering fuel for a large burning took many hands, which made it a collective act and a public statement; the crowd in the passage is described doing exactly that. Execution by fire also destroyed the body, and in a society where a man's grave and his name mattered, that was the harsher part of the sentence.
studies.didYouKnow: The command is addressed to the fire itself, in the vocative, as if to a person. The Quran does this rarely, and elsewhere it is used for the earth and the sky when they are told to swallow their water and to hold. The land Abraham is delivered to is not named here, only described as blessed for all peoples.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The rescue works by changing a property rather than by removing a threat, which is a specific kind of divine action. Nothing in the scene is undone: the crowd still decides, the fire is still lit, Abraham is still put into it. What changes is what the fire does. That leaves the human decision fully in place and its consequence entirely suspended, which is a picture of how the passage understands protection.

crossReferences.why: The same episode told again, ending with the plotters brought low.
Gives the crowd's decision and the deliverance in a single short ayah.
The whole confrontation that leads here, from the questioning to the broken idols.

studies.applyIt: Think of a situation you cannot get out of this month: the diagnosis, the job, the person you have to keep seeing. You are probably praying for it to be removed. Try praying instead for it to be made cool and safe, in those words. The passage describes a rescue that left the fire exactly where it was.

studies.title: A Grandson Given Over
studies.meaning: Two names are given as a gift, and the second is marked by a word meaning something added beyond what was asked. Commentators read it as the grandson arriving on top of the son, an extra nobody had requested. What follows describes what became of them, and the terms are all about function rather than status: made leaders who guide by God's command, inspired towards good works, and finally called servants. The line ends where it began, in service.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is moving through its gallery of prophets, and this passage covers what followed Abraham's deliverance from the fire. In a society organised entirely around descent, the note that a line continued through two named generations carried weight beyond the biography. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these two ayat.

keyTerms.note: What is given beyond what was due or asked. The word occurs twice in the Quran, once of this grandson and once of a night prayer offered over and above what is required.
From a root for the front or the intended direction. It names those others take their bearings from, and the ayah immediately limits the role: they guide by God's command, not their own.

The last word describing them, after leadership and inspiration have been mentioned. Placing it at the end makes service the category everything else sits inside rather than a stage they moved beyond.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's line was his security and his memory in Arabia. Sons meant hands for the herd, defenders in a feud and someone to keep your name in the genealogies that every family recited. A grandson meant the line was no longer contingent on one life. Being told that a second generation had been added, unasked, described the exact relief an Arabian father would have understood immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the grandson as something extra occurs twice in the Quran. The other place uses it for a night prayer offered beyond what is required, described as an addition for the one who performs it. The same term marks a voluntary act of worship and an unrequested member of a family, both defined as more than was owed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Leadership is defined here by its source rather than by its authority: they guide by God's command, which makes the role derivative. The order of the description matters too. Guidance and inspiration are listed, and then the summary is that they were servants, so the highest thing said about them is the same thing that can be said about anyone. Nothing in the passage makes their standing hereditary.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for leaders guiding by His command, and attaches it to patience and certainty.
Uses the same word for something offered in addition, of prayer in a portion of the night.
Records Abraham asking about his descendants and being told the covenant does not reach wrongdoers.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person in your family who arrived as an addition rather than a plan: a late child, a cousin who moved in, a grandparent you did not expect to know. Call or message them today for no reason. The word in this ayah exists for exactly that category, and it treats it as the better kind of gift.

studies.title: Judgement And Knowledge Given
studies.meaning: Two things are given and they are given together: the capacity to decide rightly, and knowledge. Commentators treat the pair as deliberate, since knowing what is true and knowing what to do about it are different faculties. Then a rescue is described, and the town is characterised by what it did rather than by who lived in it. The Quran states the charge briefly and moves on, without detail, which is its consistent manner with this episode.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah's gallery is moving quickly, giving each prophet a line or two. Lot's town lay on a route Arabian traders knew, and other passages note that its ruins were passed by travellers. The audience therefore knew the story as geography as well as history. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: The faculty of deciding a matter rightly. It is given here alongside knowledge and again a few ayat later to David and Solomon, so the surah treats it as a distinct gift rather than a result of learning.
A settled place rather than a tribe or a people. Naming the unit as a town makes the fault collective and located, which is how the Quran generally describes communities that were warned.
From a root for something breaking out of its shell or skin. It describes stepping outside a boundary rather than holding a wrong belief, which is why it can be said of conduct alone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hospitality was the one obligation no Arabian settlement could waive. A traveller who reached a town was owed shelter and safety, and a place that harmed its guests put itself outside the customs that made travel possible at all. Caravans depended on that guarantee across hundreds of miles. The Quran's accounts of this town elsewhere turn on exactly that breach, which the audience would have registered instantly.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of judgement and knowledge appears twice within six ayat of this surah, once here for Lot and once for David and Solomon. In the second case the surah immediately shows what having both looks like, in a dispute over a damaged field. The gallery gives the same gift twice and then illustrates it once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Rescue is presented as the ordinary outcome for the one who did not participate, and the passage spends no time on the destruction itself. What it insists on is the pairing at the start: judgement and knowledge given together, which quietly says that being right is not the same as knowing how to act. The characterisation of the town by its practice rather than its creed is equally deliberate.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same pair of gifts to David and Solomon a few ayat later, then shows them in use.
Narrates the same episode at greater length, including Lot's appeal against what his people did.
Notes that travellers pass by the remains of that place morning and night.

studies.applyIt: Notice which of the two gifts you actually lack in a decision you are avoiding. Sometimes you do not know enough, and the answer is to find out. More often you know exactly what is happening and cannot see what to do. Naming which one it is takes a minute and usually changes what you do next.

studies.title: When He Called Out Before
studies.meaning: One prophet is admitted into mercy and described as righteous, and then the surah reaches back much further. Noah is introduced not by his mission or his ark but by a single act: he called out. The response is given in three verbs, answered, delivered, supported, and the sequence begins with the answering. Commentators note that the surah's method through this whole gallery is to name the call first and the rescue second, so the calling is what the passage is about.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The gallery is compressing long narratives into single lines, and it selects from each prophet's life the moment of appeal. That selection speaks to a community under pressure with no visible prospect of relief, for whom the length of Noah's mission was the relevant fact. The word before, in this ayah, sets his call at the far end of the whole sequence. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for calling to someone at a distance, loud enough to carry. It is not the word for a quiet prayer, and the surah uses it repeatedly through this gallery for prophets in extremity.
A form that means responding to a request, with the sense of complying rather than merely hearing. The verb follows the calling immediately in the sentence, with nothing between them.
A word for anguish that presses on the chest, from a root for pressing hard. The Quran uses this phrase for the great distress three times, twice of prophets rescued from their own people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Calling out carried in the desert. A traveller separated from a caravan shouted and listened, a lost herdsman called across a valley, and the sound was the only technology available for reaching anyone. Everyone had experienced calling into a distance without knowing whether anything was there. The prophets in this surah are shown doing exactly that, and the passage is interested in what came back.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for the great distress occurs three times in the Quran. The other two are in a single surah, one of them describing the rescue of this same prophet and the other the deliverance of Moses and Aaron with their people. The Quran reserves the expression for rescues on the scale of an entire community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sequence puts answering before rescue, which separates two things people usually collapse together. Being answered is not identical with being delivered, and the passage lists them as distinct acts in order. The gallery's structure makes a further claim by repetition: across generations and utterly different circumstances, the pattern of call and response is the same, which is the surah's way of saying it is available now.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase for the great distress, of this same prophet and his people.
Applies the same phrase to the deliverance of Moses and Aaron along with their people.
Continues the same pattern later in this surah, where Job calls and is answered in the next line.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the Quran records the calling and not the wording. If you have been waiting until you can put something properly, drop that. Say the plainest version of what is wrong, out loud, once, in whatever words arrive. The passages in this surah are made of exactly that, and none of them is eloquent.

studies.title: The Sheep In The Field
studies.meaning: A dispute is introduced with no verdict attached. Two prophets are judging a case about a cultivated field into which someone's sheep strayed at night, and the verb for both of them judging is left in a form that suggests the process rather than the outcome. Then a single clause is added: We were witnesses to their judgement. The Quran does not report what either of them decided here, and the commentators note the omission before supplying their accounts of it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah gives this episode in one and a half ayat and nowhere else, and the details it withholds are supplied in the commentaries from transmitted reports, which the classical authorities pass on with varying confidence. The Meccan audience lived in a town without agriculture but traded with settlements where such disputes were ordinary. No specific occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: Cultivated ground and what grows on it, from a root for ploughing. The word covers the labour as well as the plants, which is why damage to it registers as harm to a season's work.

keyTerms.gloss: they strayed and grazed by night
keyTerms.note: This verb occurs only here in the Quran. It means specifically that animals scattered into pasture at night without a herdsman, so the ayah tells you nobody was watching them.
The word for those present at proceedings who can testify to what happened. Applying it to God as observer of the judging places the court itself under observation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Animals in a crop was among the most common disputes in any settled part of Arabia. Herds were penned at night precisely because unattended sheep would strip a field by morning, and the loss fell on a family's whole year. Custom in such cases weighed the value of the damage against the value of the flock, and the settlement was usually negotiated by elders rather than imposed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing the sheep straying at night occurs only once in the whole Quran. It is a precise pastoral term for livestock spreading into pasture after dark with nobody minding them, and the classical lexicons pair it with a separate verb used of the same animals grazing by day. The ayah chooses the word that quietly locates the negligence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is remarkable for what it withholds. Two prophets judge, the outcome is not stated, and the ayah's only comment is that the proceedings were witnessed. That places the emphasis on judging as an activity carried out under observation rather than on the correctness of a particular ruling. The next ayah will say one of them was given understanding of it, without withdrawing anything from the other.

crossReferences.why: Continues immediately, saying We gave understanding of it to one of them and knowledge to both.
Addresses the same prophet about judging between people with truth and not following desire.
States the general principle of judging between people with justice, set beside restoring trusts to their owners.

studies.applyIt: Notice the clause that ends the ayah. Someone was present at the proceedings. Next time you find yourself deciding something small about another person, their motives, whether they meant it, take ten seconds to imagine the deliberation being watched. Not to frighten yourself. It usually improves the quality of the reasoning.

studies.title: We Made Him Understand It
studies.meaning: One of the two is given understanding of the case, and the very next clause gives both of them judgement and knowledge. Commentators are careful with that sequence: the younger sees something the elder does not, and nothing is taken away from the elder for it. Then the passage moves without pause to mountains and birds made to join one of them in glorifying, and closes with three words that read like a signature: and We were the doers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is naming what each prophet was given. Both of these figures are unusual in the gallery because they held political power, and the Quran's account of them keeps returning to gifts rather than to conquests. The detail about mountains echoing praise is given in more than one surah of this period. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: This verb occurs only here in the Quran, in a form that means causing someone to understand. The insight is described as conferred rather than reached, which is why the other judge is not faulted.
A verb for putting something at another's disposal, used elsewhere of the sea, the sun and the night. It always names an arrangement made by God rather than a power held by the person.
A feminine plural verb, agreeing with the mountains. The same verb has already been used in this surah for those near God and for the sun and moon moving in their courses.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian valleys answer. A voice raised between rock walls comes back, and travellers and herdsmen used that fact deliberately, calling to locate one another across broken ground. Poets sang in wadis for the sound. An audience that had heard hills return a human voice did not need the image of mountains joining a song explained to them, though the ayah claims something more than an echo.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for being given understanding occurs only once in the Quran. The verb for glorifying, in this same ayah, has already appeared twice in this surah, first of those near God who never tire and then of the sun and moon in their courses. By this point the surah has assigned the same act to angels, to planets and to mountains.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage handles a difficult situation gently. Two people judge, one is given the better understanding, and the text immediately affirms both. That models how superior insight can be acknowledged without becoming a verdict on the other person. The wider claim is about who arranges things: understanding is granted, mountains are made to respond, and the closing phrase attributes all of it to one actor.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same detail, mountains and birds told to echo the praise along with him.
Describes the mountains glorifying with him at evening and sunrise, and the birds gathered.
Uses the same verb earlier in this surah, of those who glorify night and day without tiring.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time someone younger or less experienced saw something you missed. Notice whether you were able to say so out loud. This ayah does both things in one line: it credits the better reading and it keeps the other person whole. Try that pairing once this week, in that order, with someone who deserves it.

studies.title: Armour Against Your Own Violence
studies.meaning: A craft is described as taught rather than invented, and the purpose is stated with unusual bluntness: to protect you from your own violence. The word for you is plural and includes the listener, so the danger named is not an enemy but the hearers themselves. A question follows, asking whether they are grateful, and it is left open. Then a wind is placed at the command of the other figure, running towards a land the passage calls blessed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience lived in a peninsula where feuding was endemic and armour was expensive imported equipment. The blessed land named at the end of this ayah is the same one named earlier in the surah as the destination of Abraham's deliverance, which quietly links the two ends of the gallery. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these two ayat.

keyTerms.note: This word occurs only here in the Quran. It comes from the ordinary verb for wearing clothes, so protective mail is named as a kind of dress rather than as a weapon.
A word covering both military force and hardship. The possessive makes the audience the source of the danger, so the gift is protection from what people do to one another.
This form occurs only here. The wind put at his command is not a gentle one, which makes the arrangement a matter of a destructive force being directed rather than tamed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mail shirts were among the most valuable objects in Arabia. They were imported, repaired by specialists, named in poetry, and given as compensation in blood settlements, where a fixed number of them could close a feud. A man who owned one was wealthy. The Quran describing the making of armour as taught, and as protection from a community's own violence, spoke to an audience for whom both halves were literal.
studies.didYouKnow: The land described as blessed at the end of this passage is named with the same phrase earlier in this surah, where Abraham and Lot are delivered to it. The expression occurs four times in the Quran, and two of those are in this surah, so the same blessed destination appears at the start of the gallery and again near its end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates human danger inside the human community, not outside it, and describes a technology given as mercy against that. The question about gratitude then attaches to something people would ordinarily credit to their own ingenuity. Placing a violent wind under command in the next line makes a related point: forces that destroy and forces that protect are described with the same grammar, both arranged rather than possessed.

crossReferences.why: Names the same blessed land earlier in this surah, as the place Abraham and Lot were delivered to.
Describes iron being softened for him and the instruction to make full coats of mail.
Gives the same arrangement with the wind, running gently at his command wherever he directed.

studies.applyIt: Pick one ordinary safeguard you use without thinking: a seatbelt, a lock, a lit street. Say once, today, that it was learned rather than invented from nothing, and that most of what it protects you from is other people. The ayah's question about gratitude is left unanswered on purpose. It is waiting for one.

studies.title: You Are The Most Merciful
studies.meaning: Two prophets in two ayat, and the contrast is the point. Solomon is given divers and workers under restraint, an account of power at its widest. Then Job, with nothing, whose whole speech is six words: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful. The commentators note what is missing from it. He states his condition and names an attribute of God, and he does not ask for anything.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a passage running through prophet after prophet in short entries, each introduced with a name and a moment. Job appears here without the story attached; the details of his losses are given elsewhere. No specific occasion is reported. The passage was heard by people under a boycott, hearing a list of figures who had been at the end of their resources and were named in the same breath as a king.

keyTerms.note: The participle of guarding, used here of God over the workers given to Solomon. The same root covers protecting and confining, and the context takes it in the second sense: they were held to their task.

A verb of light contact rather than of crushing. Job describes his affliction with the gentlest available word, which is part of why the classical tradition treats the phrasing as a model of restraint in complaint.

A superlative placed over a plural of the same root, so the phrase measures God against everyone else who shows mercy. Job ends on the attribute rather than on the request, and the answer comes in the next ayah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Illness that lasted was a social sentence as much as a physical one. A person who could not work moved from provider to dependent, and a household with a long illness in it lost standing along with income. Visitors thinned out. There were no treatments for most of what people had, only waiting. The audience did not need Job's losses itemised to know what a long affliction did to a life.
studies.didYouKnow: Job's prayer is one of the shortest in the Quran and contains no request. It has been recited for centuries by people in illness, and the classical commentators frequently note that the answer given in the next ayah exceeds anything he asked for, since he asked for nothing. The surah pairs him deliberately with the wealthiest of the prophets.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Setting Solomon and Job in consecutive ayat says something the surah does not state directly. Both are described as receiving; what they receive is opposite, and neither entry ranks the other. That refuses the equation between divine favour and visible circumstance in the plainest possible way. And Job's words model a form of prayer that is not petition: naming your condition honestly and then naming God accurately, and leaving the space between them empty.

crossReferences.why: The answer in the following ayah, given as mercy and as a reminder for worshippers.
Job's story at greater length, with the spring struck for him and the oath resolved.
Jacob shows the same restraint, taking his grief to God rather than to people.

studies.applyIt: The next time you pray about something that hurts, try Job's structure exactly: say what is wrong in one sentence, then say one true thing about God, then stop. Do not add the request. It feels unfinished, which is the point. Most people have never prayed without asking, and the difference is worth feeling once.

studies.title: And Their Like With Them
studies.meaning: The answer comes in four movements and each is stated as an act. He was answered, the harm was lifted, his family was given back, and then something extra: their like along with them. Commentators differ over whether that means a second family or the same people restored and multiplied, and they set the readings side by side. The ayah then names two purposes at once, a mercy from God and a reminder addressed to everyone who serves Him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah's gallery gives each prophet a moment of appeal and a response, and this one is unusual in stating the restoration in detail. The Quran says almost nothing about the nature of the affliction, and the fuller accounts in the commentaries come largely from transmitted Israelite tradition, which the classical authorities record with varying confidence. No occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for lifting a cover off something. Suffering is pictured as a thing laid over a person rather than as a change in him, so its removal restores what was already there.
An addition beyond restoration, and the commentators read it in more than one way. What the phrasing establishes is that the answer exceeded the request, whatever the exact form.
The noun of reminding, addressed here to those who serve. The episode is preserved as something for others to remember, which makes one man's recovery a resource for people who never met him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Illness in Arabia isolated as much as it hurt. A man who could not travel or work fell out of the arrangements that made him useful to his clan, and prolonged sickness could mean a household quietly moving on without him. Recovery meant re-entry into all of that. Being given back a family, in that setting, described the restoration of a whole position rather than a private happiness.
studies.didYouKnow: The words in which this appeal is made, addressing God as the Most Merciful of the merciful, occur four times in the Quran. The other three are spoken by Moses asking forgiveness for himself and his brother, by Jacob as he entrusts a second son to the brothers who lost the first, and by Joseph forgiving those same brothers. All four come from people at the end of their resources.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is described here as exceeding what was asked, which is the passage's distinctive claim. The appeal in the previous line contained no request at all, only a statement of the situation and a name of God, and the response overshoots even that. The final word turns a private rescue into public evidence, so the point of the story is not that Job was restored but that the pattern is on record.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical address to God, spoken by Joseph as he forgives the brothers who wronged him.
Gives the fuller account of the same restoration, including the family returned and their like with them.
Contains the appeal this ayah answers, which states the affliction and asks for nothing.

studies.applyIt: Look at how the appeal in the previous line is built: here is what is happening to me, and here is who You are. No request. Try praying that way once today about the thing you are most tired of. Describe it accurately and then stop. The passage suggests the asking was never the part that mattered.

studies.title: Each One Of The Steadfast
studies.meaning: Three names are given with no story attached and one shared description: each was among those who endure. Commentators note that the surah tells us nothing about what any of them endured, which leaves the quality standing on its own. Then the second line adds what followed, and it is the same phrase used for another prophet a few ayat earlier. Admitted into mercy, counted among the righteous. Patience is the only credential the passage records.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The gallery is compressing, and these three receive a single line between them. The identity of the third figure is disputed among the classical commentators, who record several proposals about who he was and what his name meant, and settle on none. The Meccan community were themselves being asked for endurance without any promise of when it would end. No occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a root for binding something fast so it cannot move. Patience in Arabic is a holding rather than a waiting, which is why it can be the whole of what is said about a person.

A title rather than a name, appearing twice in the Quran and never explained. The root covers a share, a guarantee and taking responsibility, and the commentators record several readings of who is meant.
Described as something entered rather than received, using a verb for being admitted to a place. The same phrase was used of Lot earlier in this surah, so the gallery repeats one destination.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Endurance was the celebrated Arabian virtue and it had a physical shape. A man was praised for sitting out a siege, for holding a position in a feud across years, for keeping a promise through a drought that killed his herd. Poets measured character by what a person could bear without complaint. Naming three prophets and saying only that they endured used the highest compliment the language had.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these three names appears twice in the Quran and both times in a bare list. The third is a title rather than a name, also occurring twice, and the classical commentaries offer several explanations of who he was without agreeing. Two of the three figures the surah asks its readers to admire are people it declines to tell them anything about.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a quiet claim about what counts. Three lives are summarised by one quality, and the reward is described as entry into mercy, which is the same outcome given elsewhere in the gallery to prophets whose stories are told at length. That levelling matters: it suggests the narrative is not the point, and that endurance without an audience is fully recognised even when nothing about it is recorded.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about being admitted into Our mercy, of Lot a few ayat earlier.
Gives the only other mention of the third title, again inside a bare list of three names.
Gives the only other mention of the second name, describing him as truthful and a prophet.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you know who has held something difficult for years without it becoming a story anyone tells. A carer, a parent, a colleague. Say something to them this week that names the holding rather than the situation. This ayah suggests that is the part actually being recorded.

studies.title: The Call From The Darkness
studies.meaning: Jonah is named by a title rather than by name, the man of the whale. He left angry, thinking he would not be constrained, and the commentators are careful with that clause: it describes an assumption about being pressed, not a doubt about God's power. Then the call from inside layered darkness, and it contains no request. It affirms, it exalts, and it admits fault. The answer follows immediately, with a general rule attached.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the same run of short prophetic entries. Jonah's story sat in the memory of the region through Jewish and Christian communities, so the audience had some acquaintance with it. No specific occasion is reported. The passage was heard at a point when the messenger himself was being urged to abandon a people who would not listen, which is precisely what Jonah is described as having done.

keyTerms.note: A participle of a form that suggests anger exchanged between two parties. The commentators refer it to his people rather than to God, since the form implies a quarrel he was walking away from.
A plural, so more than one layer of dark. Commentators count them variously as the night, the sea and the belly of the creature, and the plural itself is what carries the sense of being enclosed.
A word for something that covers and presses down, used of a cloud and of grief. It names the state he was saved from as a weight rather than as a place, which the ayah then generalises.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sea was the edge of the known world for inland Arabs, and what came back from the ports were stories about men who had gone out and men who had not returned. Sailors were a distinct class, and their tales of what lived below were part of the region's common stock. A man swallowed and returned was, to that audience, the outermost case of a situation with no way out, which is exactly the use the passage puts it to.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer has been recited for centuries as a formula in distress, and its three parts are always noted in that order: there is no god but You, glory be to You, I was among the wrongdoers. It is one of the very few prayers in the Quran that ends with an admission rather than a request. The following ayah then extends the same deliverance to the believers as a general rule.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The rescue is attached to a general rule in the very next clause: thus do We save the believers. That turns a singular episode into a stated pattern, which is unusual and deliberate. What the pattern requires is visible in the prayer itself. There is no bargaining and no defence; the man says what God is and what he himself has been. Naming the fault accurately is presented as the turn, not as the price.

crossReferences.why: The same story at length, from the flight to the gourd plant and his people believing.
Instructs against being like the man of the whale, and records how he was chosen.
Notes that Jonah's people were the one town whose belief benefited it.

studies.applyIt: Say the three parts of this prayer tonight, in order, about something you got wrong recently. Do not skip the third part, which is the only one that costs anything. Notice that Jonah did not explain himself, did not describe the provocation, and did not ask to be let out. He simply named the position he was in.

studies.title: Do Not Leave Me Alone
studies.meaning: The request is made and then immediately qualified by the petitioner himself. He asks not to be left solitary, and before any answer comes he adds that God is the best of inheritors, which concedes that nothing would be lost if the request were refused. Commentators read the second clause as the shape of the prayer rather than as an apology for it. He asks for what he wants and states, in the same breath, that his hope does not depend on getting it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The gallery has been giving each prophet a moment of appeal, and this one is childless and old. In a society where a man without descendants had no continuation of any kind, the request is for the most ordinary thing and the most impossible. The Quran gives fuller versions of this prayer elsewhere. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb for leaving something behind or letting it be. It asks God not to let a situation simply continue, which is a different request from asking for an intervention.
One without a second, occurring three times in the Quran. The other two describe a person coming to God on the last day with nothing and nobody, which is the state he is asking not to be left in now.
Those who remain when someone is gone and take what he leaves. Calling God the best of them concedes the whole point of wanting an heir while still asking for one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Childlessness in Arabia was a form of erasure. Property passed to collateral relatives, a man's name dropped out of the genealogies that families recited, and there was nobody obliged to remember him or to answer for his blood. Old men without sons became dependents in other households. The word he uses for being left alone named a social condition as much as a private grief.
studies.didYouKnow: The word he uses for being left alone occurs three times in the Quran. The other two both describe a person arriving before God on the last day singular and with nothing, one of them just a few ayat from the end of an earlier surah. He asks not to be left in this life in the condition everyone will be in at the end of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer models something difficult: wanting a specific outcome and holding it loosely at the same time, without either pretending not to want it or making the want a demand. The clause about inheritance is not resignation. It is an accurate statement of the situation, offered inside the request, and the surah records that the request was answered without suggesting the qualification was what earned it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same prayer at greater length, including the fear of what would come after him.
Uses the same word for coming to God alone, of a person stripped of everything he counted on.
Records the answer in the very next line, and describes the household that resulted from it.

studies.applyIt: Take something you want badly and say it plainly to God, without softening the wanting. Then add one true sentence about how things stand if it does not come. Both halves. This prayer does not choose between hope and acceptance, and the ayah suggests you are not required to choose either.

studies.title: In Longing And In Awe
studies.meaning: The answer to Zechariah is given in three verbs and then the reason is supplied. He is answered, John is granted, and his wife is set right for him. Then the ayah steps back to describe the household rather than the miracle: they raced each other in good works, they called on God in longing and in dread, and they were humbled before Him. The commentators read the last part as explaining why the prayer was answered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the sequence of prophets with the household of Zechariah and then with Mary. No specific occasion is reported. The surah's method throughout is to give a name, a moment of extremity, and an answer, and this entry is the one that pauses to describe the people afterwards. The audience were being shown what kind of household God responds to, at a time when theirs were breaking apart.

keyTerms.note: A form that implies competing with one another rather than simply moving fast. The picture is of a household in which good works were something people got to first, which is a description of a culture rather than of individuals.
Two nouns set side by side without a verb between them, so both states are present at once rather than alternating. The classical tradition treats the pair as the balance a heart is meant to hold.

A participle used of a voice dropping, of eyes cast down, and of land lying flat before rain. It names a posture of the whole person rather than a feeling, which is why the Quran uses it of ground as well as of people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Households in that world worked as units, and a family's reputation was collective. What one member did in public attached to all of them, and children absorbed a way of living before they could name it. A description of a whole household competing in good works would have read to that audience as a description of a family's character, the way a family might be known for generosity or for its horses.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words for longing and dread appear together only here in the Quran. The verb about the wife is also unusual: it is the verb for putting something right or repairing it, and the commentators divide over whether it refers to her physical condition or to her disposition. Most report the range without settling it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah names two orientations that are usually treated as opposites and requires both at once. Longing without dread turns into presumption; dread without longing turns into despair, and the pairing keeps a heart between them. What is striking is the setting. This is not offered as advice but as the description of a family whose prayer was answered, so the balance is presented as something people lived rather than a doctrine they held.

crossReferences.why: The same episode told at length, with the sign of three nights and the news of John.
Describes sides leaving their beds, calling on their Lord in fear and hope.
Names those who race in good works and gives the state they do it in.

studies.applyIt: Pick one small good act your household already does and turn it into something you get to first this week: taking the bins out, making the tea, saying the greeting. Do not announce it. The ayah describes a family who raced each other to these things, and racing only works if somebody starts without being asked.

studies.title: A Sign For All Peoples
studies.meaning: She is introduced without a name, by an act: the one who guarded her chastity. The gallery has been naming prophets, and here it names a woman by what she did rather than by a title. Then two things are stated. Something of God's spirit was breathed into her, and she and her son together were made a sign. Commentators note the pairing carefully: the sign is the two of them, not one alone, which keeps mother and child inseparable in the claim.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Christian communities were present in Arabia, in Najran to the south and along the northern routes, and Meccans knew the outline of this account. The surah places her inside a sequence of prophets without assigning her their office, and describes her by conduct and by what was given. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah, which the surah gives in a single line.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a fortress. The verb means making something inaccessible and safe, so the description is of a defence maintained rather than of an absence of opportunity.
A phrase occurring twice in the Quran, both times of this event. The possessive marks origin rather than composition, and the commentators are careful to read it as attribution of honour.
The word used throughout the Quran for verses and for indications in nature. Applied to two people, it makes them something to be read, pointing past themselves to what produced them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman's standing in Arabia was inseparable from her family's account of her, and there was no institution to appeal to if that account went wrong. Reputation was maintained by relatives and destroyed by rumour, and the consequences fell on households rather than on individuals. An account of a woman vindicated by God rather than by her kin ran against everything that society had arranged for settling such questions.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah's long gallery of prophets is interrupted once, for a person named by an action rather than by a name. The exact phrase used here for what was breathed into her occurs only twice in the Quran, and the other place also refers to her, in a surah where she is held up alongside another woman as an example for everyone who believes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims sit together. The first is about integrity maintained under conditions the passage does not describe, and the second is about something given that could not be earned. Placing them in one sentence refuses the choice between merit and grace. The final phrase widens the audience to all peoples, so what happened to one household in one place is presented as evidence available to everyone afterwards.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about guarding and about the spirit, and names her as an example for believers.
Narrates the same event in detail, including her fear and the reassurance given to her.
Repeats that she and her son were made a sign, adding that they were sheltered on high ground with water.

studies.applyIt: Notice that she is identified here by something she did when nobody would have known otherwise. Pick one standard you keep privately and, instead of examining whether it matters, simply keep it today without comment. The ayah treats an unwitnessed integrity as the thing worth naming a person by.

studies.title: One Community, One Lord
studies.meaning: The gallery closes by addressing everyone in it at once. All of those lives are declared a single community, and the instruction that follows is the same one every messenger in the surah received. Then the record is stated plainly: they cut their affair into pieces among themselves. Commentators note the verb, which describes tearing rather than disagreeing. The passage does not dwell on it. It moves straight to the individual, whose effort is guaranteed not to be denied.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has moved through prophets separated by centuries and by entirely different circumstances, and this is its summary. Its listeners lived among Jewish and Christian communities that traced themselves to figures in that same gallery, and among Arabian tribes that traced themselves to Abraham. The claim of one community was audible to all of them. No specific occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: A word for a body of people held together by something shared. The phrase occurs twice in the Quran in this exact form, both times summarising a sequence of messengers.
An intensive form of the verb to cut, applied to their own affair. It describes a single thing being pulled into fragments rather than parties failing to reach agreement.
This noun occurs only here in the Quran. It is the opposite of thanks rather than of faith, so what is ruled out is effort going unacknowledged, not effort being punished.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian tribes were built from splits. Every large group remembered the quarrel that had separated it from a parent group, and genealogists tracked the fractures back through generations. A dispute over water or succession could produce two peoples within a lifetime. The verb used here for cutting up a shared affair described the ordinary mechanism by which Arabia had come to have so many separate names.
studies.didYouKnow: The word ruling out that anyone's effort will go unrecognised occurs only once in the whole Quran. It is built from the root that gives the word for disbelief, but in its plain sense of denying something owed, so it means ingratitude rather than unbelief. The Quran uses that root once in this direction, and it is about a human being's work being credited.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three moves happen quickly. Unity is declared as a fact about the messengers, fragmentation is recorded as a fact about their followers, and then the frame shifts to the individual. That last shift is the passage's mercy: whatever the state of the communities, one person's effort is written down and cannot be denied. The verse does not resolve the divisions. It removes the individual's dependence on them.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the identical declaration and the same account of the splitting into parties, each pleased with itself.
Gives the same instruction earlier in this surah, said to have been revealed to every messenger.
States the same guarantee differently, that the reward of one who does good is not wasted.

studies.applyIt: If you find yourself discouraged by how divided things are, in a family, a community, a field of work, read the third of these ayat again. It does not fix any of that. It says your own effort is being written down independently of it. Do one small good thing today without checking whether it fits the larger picture.

studies.title: Swarming From Every Height
studies.meaning: A prohibition is stated on a destroyed town, and the classical commentators divide over what exactly is barred: that its people will not return to the world, or that they will not turn back to God, and the works record both readings. The sentence then runs on without stopping into a second clause about a barrier opening and two peoples pouring down from every rise. The word for their movement is the one used of ants and of anything moving quickly in numbers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The two names appear only twice in the Quran, here and in an account of a barrier built by a traveller in the far north. Stories of walled-off peoples circulated in the region through Syriac and Persian channels, and the surah uses the reference without explaining it, which suggests the audience already had it. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A word for something set off limits. Applied to a destroyed town, it makes the impossibility of return a matter of prohibition rather than of circumstance, which is why the commentators differ over what is being barred.
This word occurs only here in the Quran. It names any swelling of ground, so the picture is of movement appearing over every horizon at once rather than from one direction.
A verb for moving quickly in numbers, used of animals and of crowds. It appears once more in the Quran, of people hastening from their graves towards their Lord.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Movement over the horizon was how danger arrived. A raiding party appeared first as dust above a ridge, and lookouts were posted on high ground precisely to see it early. Every settlement knew the sequence: a rise, a shape, then the count. Describing a force coming down from every rise at once removed the one advantage the whole system depended on, which was knowing which direction to watch.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for these peoples streaming down appears once more in the Quran, describing human beings hurrying from their graves towards their Lord. The word for the mounds they come over occurs only here. The surah gives one of its strangest images using a term found nowhere else and a verb it otherwise reserves for the resurrection.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a limit that cannot be crossed in one direction and an opening that cannot be closed in another. Nothing returns from what has already been settled, and something held back will be released. Between those two facts sits the reader's present, which is exactly where the surah has been placing them since its opening line. The reticence of the account is part of its effect.

crossReferences.why: Gives the only other mention of these two names, and the barrier built to hold them back.
Uses the same verb for people hurrying out of their graves towards their Lord.
Continues immediately, with the true promise drawn near and eyes fixed in horror.

studies.applyIt: Notice how little the Quran says here, and resist the urge to fill it in. Take one thing you cannot know the shape of, a diagnosis, a decision someone else is making, and practise leaving it undescribed for a day. The passage models a way of holding the unknown that does not require inventing details.

studies.title: We Were Heedless Of This
studies.meaning: The surah's opening sentence returns, and it is the same verb: something has drawn near. What follows is a single physical detail, eyes fixed open and unmoving, and then speech. Their words correct themselves mid-sentence. First they say they were heedless of this, and then they replace that with a harder admission: rather, we were wrongdoers. Commentators note the particle in the middle, which retracts the softer account and puts the sharper one in its place.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This ayah closes the arc the surah opened with, where people were described as heedless and turning away. Meccan audiences had heard the warning repeatedly by this stage and had settled into treating it as background noise. The surah does not accuse them of anything here; it quotes what they will say about themselves. No specific occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: This form occurs only here in the Quran. It describes an eye that stops moving and does not blink, the look of someone facing something they cannot process rather than something they fear.
The same word used in the surah's opening ayah of people turning away. Its return here closes a circle: the condition described at the start is named by those who were in it.
A particle that cancels the previous statement. Using it inside their own confession makes them correct themselves, upgrading heedlessness to wrongdoing without anyone else pressing them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccans knew the look this ayah describes. A caravan returning without its animals, a man carried back from a raid, news arriving at a house before anyone had prepared it. The fixed stare of someone hearing something that has not yet become real was familiar to everyone. The Quran chooses that expression rather than any description of fear, and gives it no other detail.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that opens this surah, saying the reckoning has drawn near, appears again in this ayah of the true promise. The word for the heedlessness people were in also comes from the first ayah. The surah has more than a hundred ayat between them, and it closes its argument by putting its opening words in the mouths of the people it opened by describing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The self-correction is the passage's most careful move. Heedlessness sounds like an accident and would be an excuse; wrongdoing is a claim about responsibility. By having them make the correction themselves, the Quran removes the possibility of arguing that inattention is innocent. What was described at the surah's opening as a manner of listening turns out, on their own account, to have been a choice.

crossReferences.why: Opens this surah with the same verb and the same word for heedlessness, describing the same people.
Puts nearly the same admission in the mouths of a destroyed town earlier in this surah.
Says the covering has been removed and the sight today is sharp, the same shift from inattention to seeing.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you have been calling an oversight, something you forgot, did not get round to, did not notice. Ask whether the softer word is accurate. Sometimes it is. When it is not, say the more exact word to yourself once. The correction in this ayah is made voluntarily, and doing it early costs almost nothing.

studies.title: Fuel And Those Kept Far
studies.meaning: The argument the surah has been making is settled by an outcome rather than a proof. Whatever was served alongside God ends up in the same place as those who served it, which shows what it was: had they been gods, they would not have gone in. Then the passage turns without transition to the opposite case. Those for whom good had already gone ahead from God are kept far from it, and the phrasing puts the decision earlier than anything they did.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has spent its length arguing against objects taken alongside God, and the audience maintained such objects at a sanctuary they controlled. The claim that the objects share the fate of their servants was directed at a devotion that expected protection to run the other way. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: This word occurs only here. It names small stones or debris thrown into a fire to keep it going, so the image is of material fed to something rather than of persons punished by it.
The long outward breath of someone in extremity, and also the sound of a fire drawing air. The Quran uses it three times, and it is a sound rather than a word.

A verb of going before. Placing God's good ahead of them makes the outcome the result of something already settled, which is why the passage can describe the distance as maintained rather than earned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Keeping a fire alive was daily work. Someone gathered scrub, dung and small stones-worth of debris to bank it through the night, and a household without fuel was cold and could not cook. The word used here belongs to that chore. Describing revered objects as the material shovelled in to maintain a fire was a deliberately undignified way to end a long argument about them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing what is thrown into the fire occurs only once in the whole Quran. It comes from the vocabulary of small stones and scattered debris, the material used to bank a household fire overnight, and Arabic uses a related term for pebbles. The surah's most serious verdict on the objects it has been arguing about is delivered in a word from the hearth.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refutation is made by outcome rather than by argument, which suits a surah that has already asked twice for proof and received none. On the other side, the good that goes ahead relocates the reader's security away from performance and into something prior. Holding both halves together is the passage's point: the same few lines contain the sharpest verdict in the surah and its most unconditional reassurance.

crossReferences.why: Made the demand for proof earlier in this surah that these ayat now settle by outcome instead.
Describes the good outcome and more for those who did well, with no gloom covering their faces.
Uses the same word for the groaning breath of those in the fire.

studies.applyIt: Notice the direction of the second half: the good went ahead of them. If you have been treating your standing with God as a running total you are anxiously maintaining, sit with that phrasing for a minute today. It does not remove effort. It puts something in front of your effort that your effort did not have to produce.

studies.title: They Will Not Hear It
studies.meaning: The reward is described first by a subtraction. They do not hear even the faintest sound of the fire, which is a stranger promise than distance: not that they are far from it, but that no trace of it reaches them. Then two positives. They remain in what their own selves desired, so the content is not specified and is left individual. And a fear called the greatest does not reach them either, because angels meet them with a sentence about a day they were promised.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage answers the description of the fire in the ayat just before it, and it is careful to define the reward against that background rather than in isolation. The surah's listeners were being asked to bear present hostility for something they could not see, and the promise given here concerns absence of dread as much as presence of good. No occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: This word occurs only here. It names the barely audible, a rustle or a whisper of movement, and it is the smallest unit of hearing the language has for what will not reach them.
A verb for appetite and craving, attributed here to their own selves. The reward is described as whatever each one wanted, which leaves the content unstated and personal to each.
This phrase occurs only here in the Quran. It names a dread by size rather than by cause, and the passage says only that it does not reach them, without describing what it is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sound carried far in the desert at night, and safety was often measured by what you could hear. A camp knew it was secure when the night was quiet, and every traveller had lain awake listening for hooves or voices at the edge of hearing. Being told that not even the faintest sound would reach them described security in the terms that audience actually used for it.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the phrases in this short passage occur nowhere else in the Quran: the word for the faintest sound and the name given to the greatest terror. Both describe things the people in question will not experience. The Quran coins its most distinctive expressions here for a sound nobody hears and a fear nobody feels.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is defined here largely by absence, which is a serious claim about what people actually want. Not hearing, not being reached by dread, and only then the presence of what each self desired. That order suggests relief precedes pleasure in the order of goods. Leaving the content of the desires unnamed is equally deliberate: the passage declines to describe the reward, and describes instead the conditions under which anything could be enjoyed.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same open promise, whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in.
Has angels meet them with reassurance, and promises whatever their souls desire.
Says whoever comes with a good deed is secure from the terror of that day.

studies.applyIt: Ask what would actually have to be absent for you to enjoy anything: a worry running in the background, a message you are waiting for, a low hum of dread. Name the one that is loudest today. This passage puts its removal before any description of pleasure, which is probably an accurate account of your own situation.

studies.title: Folded Like A Scroll
studies.meaning: The image is drawn from a writing room. The sky is folded the way a scroll is rolled up over what is written on it, which makes the heavens something that was unrolled and can be put away. Then the argument follows from the picture: as We began the first creation, We repeat it. Commentators note that the reasoning is not about power but about precedent. The line ends with two short statements, a promise binding on Us, and We will do it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Resurrection was the single claim Meccan opponents found most absurd, and the surah has been answering it since its opening ayah. The image chosen here comes from the world of documents rather than of nature, which in Mecca meant treaties, debts and the written records kept by scribes. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for folding cloth or rolling a scroll. Applying it to the sky treats the visible heavens as a surface that was spread out and can therefore be gathered in again.
This word occurs only here in the Quran. It names a written record kept for reference, and the commentators discuss whether it means the scroll itself or the scribe who rolls it.
A verb for doing something again, from a root for returning. The claim is not that a new creation will be made but that the same act will be performed a second time.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing in Mecca was rare and consequential. Treaties were inscribed and stored, debts were recorded where the parties could not trust memory, and a document rolled and put away marked a matter concluded. The gesture of rolling a scroll closed something. Using it for the sky told an audience that the world they were standing in was itself a document with a last line.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the scroll occurs only once in the whole Quran. It entered Arabic from the vocabulary of the surrounding empires, where written registers were kept and archived, and it is the same root behind the modern word for a register or record. The Quran describes the end of the visible world with an administrative term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument from precedent is the passage's core. Something that has already been done once is being described as repeatable, which reframes resurrection from an extraordinary claim into an ordinary inference. The closing phrase changes the register again.
