Calling it a promise binding upon Himself places the outcome under obligation rather than under mere ability, which is a stronger guarantee than power alone would be.

crossReferences.why: Makes the identical argument, that repeating the creation is easier for Him than originating it.
Uses the same verb of folding, there of the heavens rolled up in His right hand.
Answers the same objection about decayed bones with the one who produced them the first time.

studies.applyIt: Think about how you argue for something you cannot demonstrate. This ayah does not appeal to power; it points at something already done and says it can be done again. Try that structure once today with a person who doubts you about something: not a promise about the future, but an accurate account of the past.

studies.title: A Mercy To The Worlds
studies.meaning: Four short ayat that close the surah's argument. A promise is quoted from an earlier scripture, that the earth will be inherited by God's righteous servants, and the commentators differ over whether the earth means this one or the land of the hereafter. Then the message is called sufficient for people who worship. Then the sending itself is described in one clause as mercy to all the worlds. Then the whole content is reduced to one sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the closing movement of a surah named for the prophets and built as a series of their stories. The passage arrives after a description of the heavens folded like a scroll. No specific occasion is reported. Placing a universal claim about mercy at the end of a chapter that has been arguing with a hostile town gives the argument its widest possible frame.

keyTerms.note: The word means something written, and it is used in the Quran for the book given to David. Commentators also read it more widely here as earlier revealed scripture in general.
Indefinite and without qualification, so the sending is not described as containing mercy or bringing it but as being it. The construction is what makes the clause as sweeping as it is.
A plural covering every category of created being, the same word used in the opening surah of God as Lord. No limit of time, place or people is attached to it here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inheritance of land was the most consequential thing that happened to a family, and it was contested constantly. Wells, palm groves and grazing rights passed by lineage, and a clan that lost them lost everything at once. Quoting a promise that the earth would go to the righteous rather than to the strong reversed the only rule of succession the audience had ever seen operate.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about mercy to the worlds is five words in Arabic and is among the most quoted lines in the Quran, appearing on buildings and in sermons across the Muslim world. Its restrictive construction is easy to miss in translation: it says the sending was for nothing except mercy, which makes mercy the entire purpose rather than one of several.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The purpose of prophecy is stated in a single restrictive clause, and it is not conquest, correction or the establishment of an order. It is mercy, and the scope given is every world without limit, which includes the people rejecting the message as they hear it. The last ayah then reduces the content to one proposition and puts a question after it rather than a demand, leaving the response with the hearer.

crossReferences.why: Describes the messenger as grieved by their suffering and merciful to the believers.
States the same inheritance: the earth belongs to God, given to whom He wills.
Promises succession on earth to those who believe and act well.

studies.applyIt: Take one relationship where you have been technically right and unhelpful about it. The clause here says the whole point of the sending was mercy, and that is a standard you can apply to a single conversation. Say the same true thing this week in the way that costs the other person the least. Nothing else has to change.

studies.title: I Have Told You Plainly
studies.meaning: If they turn away, the instruction is not to argue further but to say two things. The first is that they have been informed on equal terms, with nothing held back and no advantage kept. The second is an admission: he does not know whether what they are promised is near or far. Commentators note how unusual the second half is. A messenger is instructed to state the limit of his own knowledge, in the middle of a warning about timing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah opened with people demanding to know when the promise would come and mocking its absence. These closing ayat answer that demand by conceding it. The Meccan years contained long stretches with no visible progress, and the community had no more information about the schedule than their opponents did. No specific occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb of formal notification, from the root for the ear. It names an announcement made so that no one can later claim not to have been told, which is the point of the phrase that follows.
An idiom for a footing where both sides know the same thing. It rules out any private reserve of information, so the warner claims no advantage over the people he is warning.
A denial of knowledge, occurring twice in the Quran and both times in this surah's closing lines. It is placed in the mouth of the one delivering the warning, not of those receiving it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Notice on equal terms was a recognised legal act in Arabia. Before hostilities, a party formally renounced an agreement so that the other side could not claim to have been attacked without warning, and the announcement had to be public and complete. Doing otherwise was treachery. The phrase used here belongs to that practice, and its force came from everyone knowing what a proper notification required.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase in which the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is instructed to say he does not know occurs in this exact form twice, and both are in these closing ayat of the surah, two lines apart. A surah that spends its length answering demands to know when ends by having its own messenger say twice that he cannot say.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two things that are usually confused: certainty about a message and knowledge of its timing. The first is asserted, the second is denied, and both are said by the same person in the same breath. That is a model of how confidence and ignorance coexist honestly. It also removes the temptation to defend a claim by pretending to information nobody has.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same denial of knowledge two lines later, about whether this is a trial for them.
Has the same instruction to say he does not know whether what is promised is near.
Uses the same idiom of equal terms, about returning a treaty openly rather than acting secretly.

studies.applyIt: Practise the two halves in one sentence today. Say clearly what you do think, and then say plainly what you do not know, without letting the second undermine the first. Most people do one or the other. This ayah puts them side by side and treats the combination as the honest position.

studies.title: Whose Help Is Sought
studies.meaning: Three ayat close the surah and none of them settles the argument. God knows what is said aloud and what is concealed, which answers the private conferring reported at the surah's opening. Then a second admission of not knowing: perhaps this is a trial and an enjoyment for a while. Finally a prayer, brief and without elaboration, asking for judgement with truth, and naming God by the same title the surah has used throughout, with help sought against what they describe.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah ends without vindication, in the middle of an unresolved confrontation, which matches the community's actual position for most of the Meccan years. The name used in the closing line is the same one that Meccans had objected to earlier in the surah, so the last word given to the messenger uses the contested name. No occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: Open, audible speech, set against what is kept back. The pair answers the surah's opening scene, where the wrongdoers were described conferring privately about what to say in public.
The word for testing metal in fire, covering both the trial and the disorder it exposes. Applied to a delay, it suggests the waiting itself may be the examination rather than an interval before one.

keyTerms.gloss: the One whose help is sought
keyTerms.note: A passive form, occurring twice in the Quran. The other place is Jacob's response when his sons bring him a story he does not believe, and both uses come at the end of a losing argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Formal appeals were how Arabs closed disputes they could not win. A wronged party who had exhausted negotiation would stand and call publicly for judgement, sometimes at the sanctuary itself, and the appeal was heard by everyone present even though no court existed to act on it. The closing prayer of this surah has that shape: a matter handed over in public, with the outcome left open.
studies.didYouKnow: The title used in the last line of this surah, the One whose help is sought, occurs twice in the Quran. The other is spoken by Jacob when his sons return with a shirt and an account of a wolf that he tells them he does not accept. Both uses are the words of someone who cannot prove what he knows.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah ends by handing the matter over rather than resolving it, which is a form of trust rather than of resignation. The admission that the situation may be a trial is important: it allows that the difficulty is purposeful without claiming to know the purpose. And the appeal for judgement with truth asks for the outcome to be correct rather than favourable, which is a harder prayer than it first appears.

crossReferences.why: Gives the only other use of this title, in Jacob's reply to an account he does not believe.
Opens this surah with the private conferring that the first of these ayat answers.
Reports the earlier objection to the same name of God that closes the surah here.

studies.applyIt: End something today the way this surah does. Take a situation you cannot resolve and say a short sentence over it asking for the true outcome rather than the one you want. Then stop working on it for the rest of the day. The surah's last move is to put a matter down, and it is not the same as giving up.
